prompt: The parks department will install one playground at Oak Street, finish on a fixed date, and then hand the site to the grounds crew. The same leaders also run a multi-year bundle of related park renovations, and a separate citywide collection of work aligned with the department's strategy. What kind of effort is the Oak Street playground?

options.text: Call it a program, because the playground sits inside a larger parks strategy
Call it a project, because it is temporary and ends when the site is handed over
Call it a portfolio, because it draws on the same capital funds as other city work
Call it an operation, because crews will maintain the finished site in later years

explanation: A project is a temporary effort that produces a unique result and then stops. The Oak Street install has a finish date and a handover, so it is one project. The multi-year bundle of related renovations is the program, and the strategic collection of efforts is the portfolio.

distractorExplanations.a: This labels the single playground as the program. A program coordinates several related projects for benefits that separate management would not produce.
distractorExplanations.c: This labels one playground as the portfolio. A portfolio is the strategic group of projects, programs, and operations, not one site with an end date.
distractorExplanations.d: This confuses the later upkeep with the install itself. Groundskeeping after handover is ongoing work; the install is the temporary effort.

prompt: Radiology staff now book patients, run scans, and restock supplies every weekday after the new imaging wing was turned over to the department. The build itself has ended. What kind of work is the weekday scanning now?

options.text: Project work, because each scan is a unique result with its own end date
Program work, because the scans are grouped so the wing captures a shared benefit
Portfolio work, because the scans must compete with other departments for equipment funds
Operations, because the scanning repeats on ordinary weekdays and has no finish date

explanation: Once the wing is handed over, booking patients and running scans is the department's ordinary repeating work. Operations continue without a planned end. The construction that created the wing was the temporary effort; that effort is already finished.

distractorExplanations.a: This treats a routine scan as a project. A project is temporary and unique; a weekday scan is repeated production of the same service.
distractorExplanations.b: This treats the daily schedule as a program. A program coordinates related projects, and these scans are not a set of projects.
distractorExplanations.c: This treats scanner time as a portfolio decision. Competing for funds may happen at budget time, but the scanning itself is ongoing departmental work.

prompt: A regulator has already published the exact report layout, the required data fields, and the filing deadline for this compliance package. The sequence of work is well known and unlikely to shift. Which development approach fits this package?

options.text: A predictive life cycle, because the requirements and the sequence are already stable
An adaptive life cycle, because the filing should be discovered one short cycle at a time
A portfolio selection review, because stable rules are a strategic funding choice
An operations handover, because work this well known no longer counts as a project

explanation: Predictive work fits when the result and the order of work can be planned up front. Here the layout, fields, and deadline are already fixed, so uncertainty is low. An adaptive cycle is for work that must emerge because the result is still unclear.

distractorExplanations.b: This picks an adaptive cycle for a stable filing. Adaptive delivery is useful when requirements are uncertain, which is not the case in this package.
distractorExplanations.c: This confuses a life-cycle choice with portfolio selection. Choosing how to build a known package is not the same as choosing which efforts to fund.
distractorExplanations.d: This treats familiar work as operations. A compliance package still has a deadline and a unique filing, so it remains a project with a predictive approach.

prompt: On a warehouse fit-out, the dock must stay open during business hours, the crew believes the rack vendor can deliver in six weeks, a permit delay has already stopped electrical work, and a storm next month might flood the unfinished floor. Which of those four facts is the risk?

options.text: The dock must stay open during business hours
The crew believes the rack vendor can deliver in six weeks
A storm next month might flood the unfinished floor
A permit delay has already stopped the electrical work

explanation: A risk is an uncertain event that may or may not happen and could affect the work. The storm is still in the future and might flood the floor, so it is the threat to record and respond to. The other three notes are a limit, a belief, and a problem that has already occurred.

distractorExplanations.a: This is a constraint, not a risk. The open dock is a limit the fit-out must live with, not an uncertain event that might occur.
distractorExplanations.b: This is an assumption. The crew is treating the six-week delivery as true for planning, and it is not an event that might happen.
distractorExplanations.d: This is an issue. The permit delay has already stopped the electrical work, so it is a current problem rather than an uncertain future event.

prompt: An associate reads the draft scope statement for a clinic scheduling system. It names the features in scope, the features out of scope, and the deliverables, but it never says how the clinic will decide the system is acceptable. What gap should the associate call out?

options.text: The business case is missing, so the charter benefits cannot be found in this draft
Acceptance criteria are missing, so completion of the system cannot be judged
The risk register is missing, so threats have nowhere to be scored and ranked
The stakeholder register is missing, so the sponsor cannot be listed by name

explanation: A scope statement describes what is in and out, the deliverables, and the acceptance criteria used to judge those deliverables done. Without acceptance criteria, the clinic has no agreed test for saying the scheduler is acceptable, even if the feature list looks complete.

distractorExplanations.a: This looks for the business case inside the scope statement. Benefits and the case belong with initiation and the charter, not in the gap this draft actually has.
distractorExplanations.c: This looks for a risk register. Threats are tracked in that register, while the hole in this statement is how acceptance will be judged.
distractorExplanations.d: This looks for a stakeholder register. Who the sponsor is belongs in stakeholder records, not in the missing acceptance language.

prompt: The museum exhibit is two weeks behind, yet a coordinator is told to tell the steering group that the work is essentially on track so the meeting stays calm. The softer wording would hide the slip. Which value in the PMI Code of Ethics is at stake?

options.text: Respect, because the steering group should be spared an upsetting schedule report
Fairness, because the vendors should hear matching calm wording in that meeting
Responsibility, because the coordinator is the person who owns the meeting agenda
Honesty, because a status update must not conceal a slip that is already known

explanation: Honesty requires truthful communication, including not withholding a fact that would make the status misleading. Calling a two-week slip 'essentially on track' is a shaded status. The steering group cannot decide well if the delay is hidden to keep the room calm.

distractorExplanations.a: This confuses respect with sparing people bad news. Respect does not mean hiding a known delay so a meeting feels easier.
distractorExplanations.b: This confuses fairness with using the same soft words. Fairness is about impartial decisions and conflicts of interest, not a calm phrase that conceals a slip.
distractorExplanations.c: This confuses responsibility with owning an agenda. The breach here is a misleading status, not who runs the steering meeting.

prompt: A buyer must award a training contract. One bidder is a close friend and submitted a weaker proposal than two qualified firms. The buyer wants to steer the award toward that friend before scoring is finished. How should the buyer handle the friend's proposal?

options.text: Disclose the friendship and leave the award so an impartial person can score the bids
Award the contract to the friend and mention the relationship after both parties have signed
Remove the two stronger firms so the friend's weaker proposal is able to win
Let the friend rewrite the price after reading what the other firms proposed

explanation: Fairness bars a personal relationship from deciding who receives a contract. A friend among the bidders is a conflict of interest, so the tie has to be surfaced and the conflicted buyer has to stay out of the scoring while someone else applies the published criteria.

distractorExplanations.b: This still steers the award to the friend and only discloses afterward. Fairness requires the conflict to be disclosed and kept out of the decision, not repaired after the signature.
distractorExplanations.c: This drops qualified firms to favor a friend. That is a personal consideration deciding a contract, which is the fairness breach itself.
distractorExplanations.d: This gives the friend the other prices. Sharing competitors' proposals so a friend can rebid is favoritism, not an impartial evaluation.

prompt: In a bridge design review, a junior analyst raises a load-path concern. The lead laughs, calls the point naive, and moves on while the room watches. The analyst goes quiet. What should the lead do next?

options.text: Email the sponsor that the analyst wasted time in the design review
Tell the analyst to stop raising concerns while the group is watching
Acknowledge the concern and give it a serious hearing on its merits
Drop the analyst from the later design reviews so the room stays light

explanation: Respect means dealing with people without ridicule and taking a raised concern seriously. Laughing off a load-path point in front of the room dismisses the analyst and can bury a real design issue. The lead should hear the concern and judge it on the engineering, not on who said it.

distractorExplanations.a: This escalates the analyst as a time-waster. That spreads the public dismissal instead of examining whether the load path is actually a problem.
distractorExplanations.b: This tells the analyst to stay silent in the group. Respect does not mean suppressing a safety-relevant concern so the review feels smoother.
distractorExplanations.d: This removes the person who spoke up. Excluding them protects the lead's tone and throws away both the concern and the analyst's place on the review.

prompt: A supplier asks the associate to leave a known guardrail defect out of the school-lab handover report so the building can open on Friday. Students would pass that rail every day. How should the associate answer the supplier?

options.text: Omit the defect from the report and mention it in a private note to the supplier
Report the defect and refuse to conceal a condition that can injure users
Hold the report until the supplier sends a photo with the rail cropped out
Pass the handover to a teammate and stay silent about the rail

explanation: Responsibility includes a duty to public safety and a refusal to hide a condition that can harm people. A known guardrail defect on a school route has to be in the handover, even if that delays Friday's opening. Concealing it so the building can open puts students at risk.

distractorExplanations.a: This still hides the defect from the formal handover. A private note does not meet the duty to surface a safety defect the users will face.
distractorExplanations.c: This waits for a cropped photo so the defect stays invisible. Delaying the paperwork to help the supplier hide the rail is still concealment.
distractorExplanations.d: This transfers the file and stays quiet. Handing the silence to a teammate does not discharge the duty to report a known hazard.

prompt: A bank will replace its teller software and deliver the new system by March. A separate group will coach branch staff, rewrite procedures, and sustain the new way of working after go-live. What is the software effort's role in that change?

options.text: It is the permanent office that will coach staff and sustain adoption after March
It is the portfolio choice that decides which branches are allowed to change first
It is the operations group that will run the teller line after the system is live
It is the temporary effort that delivers the new teller system as the change

explanation: The March software replacement exists to put a new teller system in place and then end. Coaching branch staff and keeping the new routines alive sit with the separate group that remains after go-live. Treating the delivery as that ongoing office mixes up the vehicle for the change with the people who sustain it.

distractorExplanations.a: This makes the software effort the change-management office. The separate group owns coaching and sustained adoption; the software effort does not become that office.
distractorExplanations.b: This makes the replacement a portfolio decision. Choosing which branches move first may be a portfolio or program call, not the role of this one delivery.
distractorExplanations.c: This makes the project the operations line. After go-live, teller work is operations; the project is the temporary delivery of the system.

prompt: Before anyone prices the library renovation, the sponsor asks why the team is writing a cost management plan instead of producing one budget total. No estimate has been prepared yet. What is that plan's job?

options.text: It sets the rules for how costs will be estimated, budgeted, and controlled
It stands in for the budget as the single approved total for the renovation
It lists the invoices the contractor has already submitted for this library renovation
It assigns a duration to each task so the schedule can be baselined next

explanation: The cost management plan is written before the numbers so everyone estimates and controls costs the same way. It covers units, precision, control thresholds, and how performance will be measured. The budget total comes later, after estimates are built under those rules.

distractorExplanations.b: This treats the plan as the budget figure. The plan holds the rules for estimating and control; the approved total is produced after the estimates exist.
distractorExplanations.c: This treats the plan as an invoice log. Invoices are actual costs recorded later, and none exist yet because pricing has not started.
distractorExplanations.d: This confuses the cost plan with schedule planning. Task durations belong to the schedule, not to the rules for how money will be estimated.

prompt: A software effort has two drafts on the table. One describes how the work will be executed, monitored, and closed. The other describes how the product will be positioned, priced, and improved in the market after launch. Which draft is the project management plan?

options.text: The market draft, because price and later improvements are the project controls
Both drafts, because a launch price is part of controlling the work
The draft that says how the work will be executed, watched, and closed
Neither draft, because the charter already states the rules for execution

explanation: One draft is about running this effort through to close. The other is about how the product will live in the market: position, price, and later improvement. Authorization sits in the charter and does not take the place of the document that says how the work itself will be run.

distractorExplanations.a: This swaps the product plan for the project plan. Price and a market roadmap manage the product after launch, not how the project work is run.
distractorExplanations.b: This merges the two documents. A launch price can be a product decision, and it does not turn the market draft into the plan for executing the project.
distractorExplanations.d: This replaces the management plan with the charter. The charter authorizes the effort and names the high-level intent; the management plan still has to say how the work will be run.

prompt: The schedule shows lab accreditation granted as a diamond with zero days, and it shows preparing the accreditation packet as a ten-day bar. A planner wants to put three days of duration on the diamond. What should the associate tell the planner?

options.text: Add the three days, because a line on the schedule is expected to consume time
Leave the diamond at zero duration, because a milestone marks a point in time
Convert the ten-day packet bar into a milestone so the two lines match
Delete the packet bar, because diamonds are the lines this schedule should keep

explanation: A milestone is a significant event, such as accreditation being granted, and it has no duration. The ten-day bar is the task that consumes time to prepare the packet. Putting three days on the diamond would turn an event into a task and blur the moment the accreditation actually occurs.

distractorExplanations.a: This assumes every schedule line must consume time. Tasks have duration; a milestone is a point in time and stays at zero duration.
distractorExplanations.c: This converts the real task into a milestone so the shapes match. Preparing the packet takes ten days, so it stays an activity, not an event.
distractorExplanations.d: This deletes the work that leads to the event. The schedule needs both the duration task and the zero-duration milestone that marks the grant.

prompt: Moving the records room requires archivists, a rented lift, and a stack of packing crates. The planner has placed all three on a single line called staff hours. How should the archivists, the lift, and the crates be recorded?

options.text: Record the lift and the crates as staff hours, because people are the ones who use them
Drop the crates from the plan, because materials do not count as resources on a move
Keep the rented lift and drop the other lines, because equipment covers this move
List the archivists, the lift, and the crates as three different resource types

explanation: People, equipment, and material are planned differently. Archivists are team resources, the lift is equipment, and the crates are material that gets used up. Collapsing all three into staff hours hides the rental and the consumable stock the move actually needs.

distractorExplanations.a: This keeps the collapse into staff hours. A lift is equipment and crates are material, even though people operate the lift and pack the crates.
distractorExplanations.b: This drops material because it is not labor. Packing crates are a material resource and still have to be planned and obtained.
distractorExplanations.c: This keeps equipment and drops people and material. The move needs archivists and crates as well as the rented lift.

prompt: A supplier email says a critical fitting may be discontinued next quarter. The associate posts a short warning in the team chat and is about to close the laptop without writing anywhere else. What should happen to that warning?

options.text: Add the fitting to the risk register so the threat can be analyzed and tracked
Leave it in the chat, because a team message already counts as the record
Place it on the issue log, because a possible discontinuation has already caused harm
File it in lessons learned, because the next effort is the right audience for it

explanation: A threat that may happen later belongs in the risk register, where it can be described, assessed, given an owner, and tied to a response. Chat scrolls away and is not the register. The fitting has not been discontinued yet, so this is not a current issue, and lessons learned are too late for a live threat.

distractorExplanations.b: This treats a chat line as the risk record. A message can alert people, but the threat still needs a register entry so it is analyzed and tracked.
distractorExplanations.c: This logs a future possibility as an issue. An issue is a problem that has already occurred; a fitting that may be discontinued next quarter is still a risk.
distractorExplanations.d: This parks a live threat in lessons learned. That file helps a later effort, and it does not manage a discontinuation that could hit this one.

prompt: A Thursday meeting will decide a harbor dredging permit. The associate is building the invite list from memory and might leave out the city reviewer who is allowed to approve the permit. What should the associate consult first?

options.text: The cost baseline, to see whether Thursday's meeting fits the remaining budget
The milestone list, to confirm the meeting itself has zero duration on the schedule
The stakeholder register, to invite the people who need to be in the room
The product roadmap, to see how the permit would change the market price

explanation: The stakeholder register identifies who is affected and who can decide, including a city reviewer with approval authority. Checking it before the invite goes out is how the permit decision gets the right people in the room. Memory is a weak substitute for that list.

distractorExplanations.a: This opens the cost baseline to staff a meeting. Whether the hour fits the budget does not tell you who has authority to approve the permit.
distractorExplanations.b: This checks whether a meeting is a milestone. Duration of the meeting is a scheduling detail and does not name the reviewer who must attend.
distractorExplanations.d: This opens a product roadmap for a dredging permit. Market price is not how you find the city reviewer who can approve the work.

prompt: The crew wants to mark the kiosk rollout closed after a Friday celebration. The kiosks are installed, but nobody has formally accepted them, and the support desk has no runbook. What still belongs in closure?

options.text: A second celebration, because a party is the formal act that closes the rollout
Hand the kiosks and the support runbook over to the operations desk
A new business case, because closure is the point where initiation starts again
A full redo of the estimates, because closure rebuilds the budget from scratch

explanation: Closing the rollout includes confirming the kiosks are accepted and transferring them, with the support material, to the people who will run them. A Friday party does not replace acceptance or the runbook. Until operations can take the kiosks, the work is not closed.

distractorExplanations.a: This treats a celebration as acceptance. A party can mark the end socially, and it does not hand the product to the desk that must support it.
distractorExplanations.c: This restarts initiation at closure. A business case belongs when an effort is being authorized, not as a substitute for handing over a finished rollout.
distractorExplanations.d: This rebuilds the budget at the end. Closure does not re-estimate the work; it finishes acceptance, transfer, and release of the team.

prompt: The sponsor has approved the pharmacy relocation budget and is championing the move with leadership. A coordinator now asks that sponsor to sequence the moving tasks and name an owner for each crate. Who should sequence those tasks?

options.text: The sponsor sequences the tasks, because approving funds includes ordering the work
The operations desk sequences the tasks, because it will run the pharmacy later
The coordinator sequences the tasks, because asking the question transfers the role
The project manager sequences the work; the sponsor funds and champions the move

explanation: Funding and public championship are the sponsor's part of this relocation. Ordering the crates and naming who moves them is delivery planning. That planning belongs with the person accountable for getting the pharmacy moved, not with the person who approved the money.

distractorExplanations.a: This folds sequencing into the act of funding. Approving the budget does not make the sponsor the person who orders tasks and assigns crates.
distractorExplanations.b: This gives sequencing to the future operators. The desk that will run the pharmacy later is not the role that plans the move's task order.
distractorExplanations.c: This treats a question as a transfer of role. The coordinator asking does not make the coordinator the project manager who owns the sequence.

prompt: During the morning huddle, the sponsor begins assigning coding tasks to developers for the current iteration. The developers had already pulled their own work from the board. Who should assign those coding tasks?

options.text: The team executes and owns those tasks; the sponsor does not assign them
The sponsor assigns the tasks, because championship includes dispatching the work
The person leading the effort should write the code to keep control of the board
The operations lead assigns the tasks once the charter has been signed

explanation: The developers had already taken the iteration's work from the board, which is execution sitting with the people doing the code. Championship is support and resources. Using the huddle to hand out tasks steps into that execution and is not part of funding the effort.

distractorExplanations.b: This treats championship as the right to dispatch tasks. Supporting the effort is not the same as assigning the iteration's coding work.
distractorExplanations.c: This moves the work onto the person leading the effort. Writing the code to 'keep control' takes execution away from the team that already owns the board.
distractorExplanations.d: This gives assignment to operations because a charter exists. Signing a charter does not make the operations lead the dispatcher of iteration tasks.

prompt: Two developers are blocked because an access request has not been granted. The person leading the effort, who used to write code, offers to build the remaining module alone over the weekend and skip the access issue. What should that person do about the blocked module?

options.text: Build the module alone, because leading the effort means producing the product personally
Ask the sponsor to build the module, because a champion is there to deliver the code
Clear the access blocker and let the developers build the remaining module
Drop the module from scope, because a blocked task should be abandoned

explanation: The useful move is to make it possible for the developers to finish, starting with the access they are waiting on. Producing the code personally over a weekend leaves that blocker in place and pulls the module off the people who were meant to build it.

distractorExplanations.a: This equates leading with personally producing the product. Building the module alone skips the access problem the developers are actually waiting on.
distractorExplanations.b: This assigns the code to the sponsor. A champion provides support and resources; the sponsor is not the person who writes the remaining module.
distractorExplanations.d: This cancels the module because it is blocked. A blocker is something to remove, not a reason to drop agreed work from scope.

prompt: On the same morning, the associate names a clear outcome for the ward move, that patients will not wait in the hall, and also checks that yesterday's punch list was updated in the tracker. Which of those actions is leadership?

options.text: Checking the punch list, because control of the tracker is what leadership means
Naming the patient outcome, because leadership is the act of setting direction
Both actions, because setting direction and checking the tracker are one duty
Neither action, because direction on a ward move belongs to the steering group

explanation: Leadership sets direction: here, the outcome that patients will not wait in the hall. Management controls the work, which is what checking yesterday's punch list in the tracker does. Both actions can be useful on the same morning, and they are not the same kind of act.

distractorExplanations.a: This calls a control check leadership. Updating and inspecting the punch list is management of the work, not the act of setting direction.
distractorExplanations.c: This collapses direction and control into one duty. They often sit with the same person, and they remain different actions.
distractorExplanations.d: This says the associate cannot set direction. Leadership of the move is not reserved to a steering group; naming the outcome is the leadership act in this pair.

prompt: A teammate presents a late shop drawing. The associate feels a flush of irritation and nearly corrects that person in front of the room, then pauses, notices the irritation, and asks a question instead. What skill is that pause?

options.text: Cost control, because irritation is a signal that the drawing overran its budget
A risk workaround, because the late drawing has already become an open issue
Scope baseline control, because the question freezes the drawing's requirements
Emotional intelligence, shown by noticing the irritation before speaking

explanation: Emotional intelligence here is self-awareness plus self-management. The associate notices their own irritation and chooses a question instead of correcting the teammate in front of the room. The pause is about the associate's reaction, not about the drawing's budget, risk log, or scope baseline.

distractorExplanations.a: This reads irritation as a cost variance. A feeling during a review is not evidence that the shop drawing overran its budget.
distractorExplanations.b: This labels the pause as a risk workaround. A workaround is a response to a threat or issue; noticing your own reaction is a different skill.
distractorExplanations.c: This treats the question as freezing scope. Asking a question before a public correction does not baseline the drawing's requirements.

prompt: The risk plan states that if the tower-crane permit is denied, the crew will switch to a pre-approved night lift with vendor B. The denial arrives at 4 p.m., and two people start inventing a different strategy in the hallway. What should the crew do with the denial?

options.text: Carry out the planned night lift with vendor B instead of inventing a new strategy
Ignore the written plan and adopt whichever hallway idea draws the most voices
Record the denial as an assumption and leave the original tower-crane booking unchanged
Close the effort, because a denied permit removes the need for any response

explanation: When a risk event hits and a response was already chosen, the crew uses that response. The plan named a pre-approved night lift with vendor B if the permit was denied, and the denial has arrived. A new strategy invented in the hallway skips the decision the plan already made.

distractorExplanations.b: This replaces an agreed response with the loudest new idea. Improvising in the hallway throws away the trigger and the response the plan already approved.
distractorExplanations.c: This files a realized event as an assumption and keeps the original booking. The denial has happened, so the contingent response is due, and an assumption is not what just occurred.
distractorExplanations.d: This closes the effort because the permit was denied. The plan already contains a way to continue; a denied permit is the trigger, not the end of the work.

prompt: A director wants a detailed Gantt chart this week for a branch-library shift that has no charter. Nobody has written why the shift matters or which benefit it should produce. Where should those benefits be named?

options.text: On the Gantt chart, because a schedule bar is where intended benefits are stored
At the closing celebration, because benefits are confirmed when the party is over
During initiation, in the charter, before the branch-library schedule is built
On the product price list, because a benefit is a claim about what the shift will cost

explanation: Initiation is where the effort is authorized and the reason for doing it is named, including the benefit the shift should produce. The charter carries that intent. A detailed schedule is planning work that comes after, so a Gantt chart this week would run ahead of the decision the charter still has not made.

distractorExplanations.a: This stores benefits on schedule bars. A Gantt chart shows when work happens; it is not the place that first names why the shift is worth doing.
distractorExplanations.b: This waits for a closing party to name benefits. Closure can confirm what was achieved, and the intended benefit has to be named when the effort is authorized.
distractorExplanations.d: This puts benefits on a price list. Cost and price are not the statement of why the library shift matters.

prompt: A forty-minute discussion of the lobby mural color ends with no decision and with no person named to finish the choice. People offered opinions and then left. Was that mural discussion an effective meeting?

options.text: Effective, because the people present had a chance to offer an opinion
Ineffective, because it produced neither a decision nor an owner
Effective, because forty minutes matches a normal status-meeting length
Ineffective, because a sponsor was not identified as present in the room

explanation: A meeting called to settle the mural color needed a decision and a person accountable for finishing it. Opinions without either result mean the time did not do the job. Length and who spoke are not substitutes for an outcome and an owner.

distractorExplanations.a: This scores the meeting on airtime. Hearing opinions can be useful, and the discussion still failed because nobody decided and nobody owned the next step.
distractorExplanations.c: This scores the meeting on the clock. Matching a familiar forty-minute length does not make a meeting effective when it ends with nothing decided.
distractorExplanations.d: This invents a missing sponsor as the failure. The discussion is ineffective because it has no decision and no owner, whether or not a sponsor was in the room.

prompt: Night-shift mechanics at the bus garage need fifteen minutes tomorrow to say what they finished, what they will do next, and what is blocking them. Which technique should they use for those fifteen minutes?

options.text: A focus group, because customers should react to the blockers in that short slot
A brainstorm, because the mechanics should invent new goals at the start of the shift
A benefits workshop, because each morning should rename why the work matters
A daily standup, because the need is a short coordination check among the crew

explanation: A daily standup is a short coordination check: finished work, next work, and blockers. Fifteen minutes for the night-shift mechanics matches that use. A focus group collects stakeholder reactions, and a brainstorm generates ideas, which this slot is explicitly not for.

distractorExplanations.a: This schedules a focus group for a crew check. A focus group is a facilitated discussion of stakeholder or customer reactions, not a fifteen-minute blocker round.
distractorExplanations.b: This schedules a brainstorm to invent goals. Brainstorming generates ideas, and the mechanics asked to report progress and blockers, not to create new goals.
distractorExplanations.c: This turns the slot into a benefits workshop. Naming why the work matters belongs with initiation, not with a fifteen-minute coordination check.

prompt: A two-person internal refresh of the staff directory is being planned with the full document set of a multi-year federal contract, including a formal procurement plan and a claims procedure. How should the planner treat that document stack?

options.text: Keep the documents this small internal refresh actually needs, and drop the rest
Produce the federal-contract document set so the two efforts look the same on paper
Skip documentation entirely, because internal work is not managed as a project
Replace the directory refresh with a portfolio scoring session instead

explanation: Tailoring means fitting the process and the documents to the effort in front of you. A two-person internal directory refresh does not need the procurement plan and claims procedure of a multi-year federal contract. It still needs the few documents that help this small effort, not a blank shelf and not a copied contract stack.

distractorExplanations.b: This copies a large contract's paperwork onto a tiny internal refresh. Matching another effort's document list is the opposite of fitting the work.
distractorExplanations.c: This drops every document because the work is internal. Tailoring reduces the stack to what is useful; it does not erase project management because the audience is internal.
distractorExplanations.d: This replaces the refresh with portfolio scoring. Selecting investments is a different decision, and it does not answer which documents this directory refresh needs.

prompt: On an adaptive member portal that starts Monday, one planner wants the screen layouts frozen today. On a predictive bridge repair whose scope was baselined last month, another planner wants that scope left undefined. Which response uses progressive elaboration correctly?

options.text: Freeze the portal screens today and leave the bridge scope undefined
Keep both efforts undefined so either one can shift without a new decision
Let portal detail emerge with learning, and keep the bridge baseline defined
Freeze both efforts completely today so later facts cannot revise either design

explanation: Progressive elaboration adds detail as more is known. On an adaptive portal, screen design is not pretended complete on day one; it emerges from early releases. On a predictive bridge job, scope that was baselined stays defined, and a change to that baseline goes through change control rather than being left blank.

distractorExplanations.a: This freezes the adaptive design too early and un-defines a predictive baseline. That reverses elaboration on both efforts.
distractorExplanations.b: This leaves both efforts undefined. Adaptive detail may emerge, and a predictive scope baseline is not left open so it can shift without a decision.
distractorExplanations.d: This freezes both on day one. The bridge baseline should stay defined, and the adaptive portal should not pretend every screen is known before any release.

prompt: The associate holds a sheet of raw percent-complete figures for twelve fiber-install tasks and is about to email that sheet to the sponsor. Nobody has compared the figures with the baseline or written what they mean. What is wrong with sending the sheet now?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because a sheet of percent-complete figures is already the report
The sheet is raw data and should be turned into a report before it is sent
The figures belong in the stakeholder register, next to each person's full contact line
The sponsor should receive the risk register in place of any performance numbers

explanation: Raw percent-complete figures are work performance data, the unprocessed observations from the work. A sponsor needs a work performance report: those figures analyzed against the baseline and compiled so the meaning is clear. Sending the sheet now presents data as if it were already that report.

distractorExplanations.a: This calls the raw sheet a report. Percent complete with no comparison and no interpretation is still data, not the compiled status a sponsor uses to decide.
distractorExplanations.c: This files performance numbers on the stakeholder register. That register identifies people and their stakes; it is not where task progress is reported.
distractorExplanations.d: This substitutes the risk register for performance reporting. Risks and progress are different records, and the sponsor still needs the progress interpreted.

prompt: A developer adds a live-chat widget that the dental booking site never requested, hoping the extra feature will impress the sponsor. No change request was filed, and the widget sits outside the agreed scope. What should happen to the live-chat widget?

options.text: Keep the widget, because an unrequested feature is extra value at no charge
Hide the widget until closure so the extra work stays off the status notes
Ask the sponsor to sequence the widget as a personal task on the board
Stop building the extra widget and route the idea through a change request

explanation: Gold plating is extra scope nobody agreed to, slipped in to impress someone. The widget was never part of the booking site that was accepted, so it cannot stay as a quiet gift. Change control is how an idea like that gets a yes, a no, or a later date, with the sponsor able to see it.

distractorExplanations.a: This treats gold plating as free value. An unrequested widget still consumes time, can affect the release, and bypasses the decision the change process exists to make.
distractorExplanations.b: This hides the extra work until closure. Keeping it off the status notes conceals a scope change instead of putting it through a request.
distractorExplanations.c: This asks the sponsor to sequence the widget as a personal task. Sequencing does not authorize scope, and the sponsor is not the person who should quietly adopt an extra feature.

prompt: City clerks sketched a mobile app for parking citations before anyone asked why residents abandon the payment website. Notices still pile up because staff retype each one from a paper pad. What should the analyst do before any screen is designed?

options.text: Assess why citations fail today, from the website drop-off through the retyping, before choosing an app
Treat the sketched mobile app as the committed requirement and open screen design with the clerks this week
Turn each whiteboard screen into a user story and hand that set to development to start building
Rank citation-app vendors by the annual license price and award the work to the cheapest bid

explanation: Needs assessment comes before a solution is chosen. Residents leaving the website and clerks retyping paper notices are the problem to confirm. The sketch is one possible response, and it may automate the wrong step if the failure sits in the website or in the retyping.

distractorExplanations.b: Opening screen design treats an untested sketch as the solution. The clerks have a preferred app, not a confirmed account of why citations fail.
distractorExplanations.c: Stories written from undiscussed screens lock a design. They describe a solution before the citation failure is understood.
distractorExplanations.d: License price is a purchase step after the need is known. The cheapest app can still miss the retyping work that is piling up notices.

prompt: A sponsor wants a $400,000 gift-shop kiosk because a board member liked one at another hospital. The draft case shows three years of costs above any realistic sales lift, and the staffed counter already breaks even. What recommendation belongs in that case?

options.text: Proceed, and trim the cost lines so the board packet presents a more favorable payback story
Proceed with a smaller kiosk and leave this unfavorable case on file without a new analysis
Do not proceed, because the case does not show benefits that cover the kiosk spend
Replace this shop's sales figures with the other hospital's results and submit the case again

explanation: A business case is the comparison that justifies spending money. Here the costs stay above any realistic sales lift, and the staffed counter already breaks even, so the kiosk is not supported. The honest recommendation is not to proceed, rather than adjusting the story to protect a board member's preference.

distractorExplanations.a: Trimming cost lines to improve the payback story hides the result the draft already shows. A case that does not support the spend should not be rewritten to look as if it does.
distractorExplanations.b: A smaller kiosk is a different proposal. Proceeding while the current case stays unfavorable spends money the analysis does not justify.
distractorExplanations.d: Another hospital's sales are not this shop's benefits. Substituting them makes the case describe a different operation.

prompt: Advisors wrote down two transcript operations. Clerks stamp paper forms and the registrar mails copies days later. Separately, a student would download an official copy the same day without visiting the desk. A colleague filed the download note under problems with today's desk. Which label fits the download note?

options.text: Current state, because a student can already download an official transcript while standing at the paper desk
Future state, because same-day download is the operation wanted, not the mailing desk as it works now
Gap list, because a download link is a set of developer tasks rather than a target operation
Business rule, because same-day copies constrain the way clerks stamp and mail the paper forms

explanation: Current state is the operation that exists now: stamped forms and mailed copies. Future state is the operation the registrar wants: a same-day download without a desk visit. The download note describes that target, so filing it as a problem with today's desk swaps the two pictures.

distractorExplanations.a: The download is not happening at the paper desk. Calling it current state treats the desired operation as if the mailing desk already worked that way.
distractorExplanations.c: A gap is the difference between the two operations, not the future operation itself, and a download is not a list of developer tasks.
distractorExplanations.d: A business rule would constrain how work is allowed to proceed. Same-day download describes a target operation, not a constraint on stamping forms.

prompt: Warehouse leads described counts on clipboards, tallies at the end of the shift, and a weekly spreadsheet. They also described scanners updating the inventory record as each aisle is finished. A developer rewrote that difference as three screens and an API. What is the gap?

options.text: The three screens and the API, because those build tasks are the difference the warehouse must close
The weekly spreadsheet by itself, because that file is the record the leads say they trust today
The scanner vendor's feature brochure, because the product list defines the capability that is missing
Clipboard end-of-shift tallies versus scanners that update the record as each aisle finishes

explanation: Gap analysis is the difference between the current operation and the future one. Today the warehouse tallies on clipboards and a weekly spreadsheet. The target is a scanner update as each aisle is finished. Screens and an API are one way a developer might close that gap, not the gap itself.

distractorExplanations.a: Screens and an API are solution tasks. They may be how someone builds toward the future state, but they are not the difference between the two operations.
distractorExplanations.b: The spreadsheet is one piece of today's count, not the difference between the two operations. A gap includes both the clipboard tallies and the scanner update as each aisle finishes.
distractorExplanations.c: A vendor brochure lists what a product can do. It does not state the difference between today's tally and the aisle-level update the leads described.

prompt: A single compounding pharmacist can explain why certain recipes skip the automated counter and go to the bench. Colleagues repeat a shorter account that leaves those exceptions out. The requirement will be wrong without that depth. How should the analyst get those exceptions?

options.text: A one-to-one interview with the pharmacist who knows why those recipes leave the counter
A workshop with every department that touches the store, aimed at a shared written policy
A survey of the cashiers who ring up finished prescriptions at the front counter
Watching the dock where wholesale totes are unloaded, without speaking to the pharmacist

explanation: An interview is how you get depth from the one person who holds the exceptions. Colleagues already repeat a shorter account that drops the recipes leaving the counter for the bench. A group session would smooth over the cases this requirement depends on.

distractorExplanations.b: A workshop fits when several groups must agree. This situation needs one expert's exceptions, not a store-wide policy session.
distractorExplanations.c: Cashiers see finished prescriptions, not the bench exceptions. A survey would collect the shorter account the analyst already knows is incomplete.
distractorExplanations.d: The dock is the wrong place. Unloading totes will not show why a recipe leaves the automated counter for the bench.

prompt: Fire, zoning, and health each reject building permits with a different checklist, and applicants leave with three conflicting lists. No single inspector can settle a shared list for the other two groups. The analyst needs one list all three will honor. How should that shared list be created?

options.text: Interview the fire marshal in private and publish that version as the list the others will use
Watch one applicant complete a form, with none of the three inspection groups in the room
Hold a workshop in which fire, zoning, and health write one shared checklist together
Show a clickable permit-portal prototype before the three groups have agreed on the list

explanation: A workshop is used when several groups must agree, not when one expert's private knowledge is enough. Fire, zoning, and health each reject permits for different reasons, and no inspector can bind the other two. Building the checklist in one facilitated session is how a single list becomes something all three will honor.

distractorExplanations.a: A private interview captures the fire marshal's depth and then imposes it. Zoning and health have not agreed, so applicants will still meet conflicting lists.
distractorExplanations.b: Watching an applicant shows how a form is filled. It does not create agreement among the three inspection groups.
distractorExplanations.d: A prototype presents a solution. The groups have not agreed on the checklist the portal would enforce, so the screen would freeze the conflict.

prompt: Front-desk agents report that they offer a late checkout when a room is empty. On a tour-group morning last month, rooms were empty and the agents did not make the offer. The spoken account and the behavior on the desk do not match. How should the analyst check what the desk actually does?

options.text: Interview the same agents again and ask them to restate the late-checkout policy from memory
Observe the desk during another tour-group arrival and record whether the offer is made
Run a workshop so the agents can rewrite the late-checkout policy as a new shared slogan
Build a checkout prototype before anyone has watched an arrival at the desk

explanation: Observation is the elicitation approach when what people do differs from what they say. The agents describe an offer on every empty room, but a tour-group morning showed the offer skipped while rooms were empty. Watching the next arrival records the practice. Another conversation would collect the spoken account again.

distractorExplanations.a: Another interview asks for the policy in words. The mismatch is between that account and the behavior, so restating the policy does not show what the desk does.
distractorExplanations.c: A workshop can rewrite a slogan. It does not test whether agents offer late checkout when a tour group arrives.
distractorExplanations.d: A prototype asks people to react to a design. The open question is the live arrival behavior, which nobody has watched yet.

prompt: Gallery visitors cannot explain how they pick a route through the museum. Asked directly, they say they wander and cannot name a decision. Interviews and a group meeting produced those same vague phrases. What should the visitors be shown so the route decision can be captured?

options.text: A longer interview guide with more open questions about wandering and route choice
A survey that asks visitors to rank the same vague phrases collected in the meetings
A business case that prices a finished mobile guide before the route need is clear
A rough prototype of the route choice that visitors can try, react to, and correct

explanation: A prototype is used when people cannot describe the requirement in words. Visitors say they wander and cannot name the choice, and further questions produced the same phrases. Something they can try gives them a way to show the choice they cannot name, which is how the missing requirement becomes visible.

distractorExplanations.a: More open questions repeat an elicitation method that already failed. The visitors could not name the decision when asked directly.
distractorExplanations.b: Ranking the same vague phrases measures preference among unclear statements. It does not surface a requirement the visitors cannot describe.
distractorExplanations.c: Pricing a finished guide commits money before the need is known. A business case does not help visitors show a choice they cannot put into words.

prompt: A librarian submitted this sentence for the baseline: the hold list shall be stored in a named vendor's tables and refreshed by a nightly batch job. Patrons need to see which branch has the book and when it will be ready. The analyst is reviewing the sentence before it enters the baseline. How should that sentence be handled?

options.text: Reject it as a design and restate the need: patrons can see the branch and the ready time
Accept it, because naming the vendor tables and the batch job makes the patron need testable
Reclassify it as a nonfunctional requirement about how fast the hold page loads
Split it into two functional requirements, one for the vendor tables and one for the nightly batch

explanation: A requirement states the need. A solution states one way to meet it. Vendor tables and a nightly batch are a design for storage and refresh. Patrons need to see which branch has the book and when it will be ready. The sentence should be rejected as a design and rewritten as that need.

distractorExplanations.b: A product name and a batch job do not make a need testable. They prescribe an implementation and leave the patron outcome out of the baseline.
distractorExplanations.c: Page-load speed is a quality attribute the librarian did not state. The sentence is a storage design, not a performance target.
distractorExplanations.d: Splitting the vendor and the batch into two sentences still records a design. Neither half states what the patron must be able to see.

prompt: Claimants have to upload accident photos from the claim file. The same page has to stay usable on a phone when the connection is slow. A writer filed both sentences as the same kind of behavior. Which sentence is the nonfunctional requirement?

options.text: The claimant can upload accident photos from the claim file
The adjuster can open those uploaded photos from the same claim file
The upload page stays usable on a phone when the connection is slow
The claimant can label each photo with the vehicle area it shows

explanation: A functional requirement states behavior the solution must provide, such as uploading a photo, opening it, or labeling it. A nonfunctional requirement states a quality of that behavior. Staying usable on a phone over a slow connection is a quality constraint on the upload page, so it is the nonfunctional sentence.

distractorExplanations.a: Uploading photos from the claim file is behavior. That is a functional requirement, which is why it does not belong in the quality bucket.
distractorExplanations.b: Opening the photos is another behavior, for the adjuster rather than the claimant. A different actor does not turn a function into a quality attribute.
distractorExplanations.d: Labeling a photo with a vehicle area is something the claimant can do. It is behavior, not a constraint on usability or speed.

prompt: A shopper story reads: as a customer I want a substitute when the store is out of my item, so I still receive a usable product. The team cannot agree on what usable means, so nobody can tell when the story is met. What is missing from the story?

options.text: A roadmap theme called Substitutions, spanning the next four planning quarters
Acceptance criteria that say how anyone will know a substitute counts as usable
A data model of shoppers, items, and the substitute products offered at the shelf
A schedule network that places this story after every other checkout task

explanation: Acceptance criteria state how anyone will know the story is met. The story promises a usable substitute and the team cannot agree what usable means, so there is no shared way to accept the work. Criteria turn that disputed word into conditions a reviewer can apply.

distractorExplanations.a: A roadmap theme places substitutions on a longer timeline. It does not tell the team when this story has been met.
distractorExplanations.c: A data model would show how shopper, item, and substitute records relate. It does not define the conditions for accepting the story.
distractorExplanations.d: A schedule network sequences tasks. Putting the story after other checkout work does not say what a usable substitute is.

prompt: One story would let parents pay school fees, track the bus, message the driver, excuse an absence, and download report cards. The team cannot put an estimate on it, and any one of those capabilities could be delivered without the other four. What should the analyst do with this story?

options.text: Keep it as one card so parents see fees, the bus, messages, absences, and cards together
Leave it whole and accept a rough guess, because a large number still lets planning continue
Redraw it as entities for fees, buses, messages, absences, and report cards
Split it, because a bundle of five features is not small and not independent

explanation: INVEST says a story should be small enough to estimate and independent enough to deliver on its own. This card bundles five capabilities, the team cannot estimate it, and each capability can ship without the others. The analyst should split it into separate stories rather than protect the bundle.

distractorExplanations.a: One card is convenient for a parent overview, but convenience does not make five features small or independent. The team still cannot estimate the bundle.
distractorExplanations.b: A rough guess papers over a story that is too large to estimate. INVEST asks for a split, not a larger number that lets planning look busy.
distractorExplanations.c: Entities for fees, buses, and messages are a data model. The problem is the size and coupling of the story, not the shape of the records.

prompt: Specialist referrals were being double-booked, which is why a requirement forbids confirming the same slot twice. A named test checks that rule. A new teammate cannot see either link and plans to drop the requirement as extra. Which artifact shows the origin and the covering test?

options.text: A traceability matrix linking the double-booking need, the requirement, and the test
The sprint backlog, which lists the referral screen the crew committed to build next
A wireframe of the referral screen that shows layout and color but not origin or test
An affinity diagram that groups workshop notes and does not point at a test

explanation: A requirements traceability matrix records why a requirement exists and which test covers it. This rule exists because specialists were double-booked, and a named test checks that a slot cannot be confirmed twice. Without that link, a new teammate can mistake a needed control for extra scope.

distractorExplanations.b: The sprint backlog is the near-term commitment. It does not show why the double-booking rule exists or which test covers it.
distractorExplanations.c: A wireframe elicits layout comments. Color and field placement do not record the origin of the requirement or the test that covers it.
distractorExplanations.d: An affinity diagram clusters raw notes into themes. It is not the link from need to requirement to test.

prompt: Transit leadership wants contactless fares in spring, monthly passes in summer, and employer accounts in the fall, laid out across the year. Separately, the crew committed to a small set of stories for the next two weeks. A coordinator calls the year-long view the sprint backlog. What is that year-long view?

options.text: The sprint backlog, because any dated list of fare work is this iteration's commitment
A data model, because spring, summer, and fall show how fare, pass, and employer-account records relate
A product roadmap, because it shows direction across the year rather than this iteration's commitment
Acceptance criteria, because spring, summer, and fall state when a single story is done

explanation: A product roadmap is direction over time: contactless fares, then passes, then employer accounts across the year. The sprint backlog is the small set of stories the crew committed to for the next two weeks. Calling the year-long view a sprint backlog collapses a multi-release direction into one iteration's commitment.

distractorExplanations.a: Dates do not make a list a sprint backlog. The two-week commitment is the backlog. The year view was not accepted as this iteration's work.
distractorExplanations.b: Seasons are a sequence of outcomes, not relationships among fare, pass, and account records. That relationship would be a data model.
distractorExplanations.d: Acceptance criteria say how one story is known to be met. Spring, summer, and fall are release horizons, not the pass conditions of a single story.

prompt: The online-order backlog contains a loyalty defect that drops earned points, a font change the owner's cousin requested, and a fraud check that could reject legitimate orders. In the review the cousin spoke longer than anyone else and insisted the font go first. How should the analyst order the next slice of work?

options.text: Put the cousin's font change first, because the longest speech in the review is the priority rule
Put the points defect and the fraud check ahead of the font, based on value and risk
Order the three items by how recently each was requested, so the newest ask wins
Give the font, the defect, and the fraud check equal shares of the next slice

explanation: Backlog order follows value and risk, not who spoke longest. Dropped loyalty points are lost value, and a fraud check that can reject real orders is a risk. The font change is a preference from the loudest voice in the room. The next slice should put the defect and the fraud check ahead of the font.

distractorExplanations.a: Speech length is not a priority rule. The cousin's insistence would bury a points defect and a fraud risk under a font change.
distractorExplanations.c: Recency is another stand-in for volume of asking. A new font request does not outrank lost points or a check that can block real orders.
distractorExplanations.d: Equal shares ignore the difference in value and risk. The font would consume the same slice as the defect that drops points.

prompt: The cent-balance check on a payroll deposit file was accepted as a must-have, because an unbalanced file pays the wrong amounts. To protect the release date, writers relabeled that check as a should-have, and the file would go to the bank without it. Employees are paid from that file. How should the analyst treat the check?

options.text: Ship without the balance check, because a should-have may be dropped once the release date is public
Relabel the check a could-have so the release notes stay shorter and the date still holds
Drop the check and rely on the bank to catch an unbalanced file after employees are paid
Keep the check in this release, because a must-have is not a should-have that can be dropped

explanation: In MoSCoW, a must-have is required for the release to meet its purpose, and a should-have is not. The balance check was accepted as a must because an unbalanced file pays the wrong amounts, and employees are paid from that file. Relabeling it to protect a date does not change that. The check stays in this release.

distractorExplanations.a: A should-have can be debated when a date is tight. This check was a must-have. A new label does not make an incorrect payroll file acceptable.
distractorExplanations.b: Could-have is a lower MoSCoW class than should-have. Moving the check down another step still drops a control the release needs.
distractorExplanations.c: A downstream bank review is not a substitute for the must-have. The file is what pays employees, so a miss is already a wrong payment.

prompt: The team keeps settling feature arguments with a card named Dana. Dana is the office manager's nickname, and every habit on the card comes from that one person. No one has interviewed a broader group or watched another office. How should this card be classified?

options.text: Not a persona yet, because a persona is a researched stand-in for a user group, not one nickname
A finished persona, because a real employee's nickname is the usual stand-in for the whole user group
A use case, because a nickname names the main actor and implies a goal for the features
A traceability matrix, because the card already links Dana to every feature argument

explanation: A persona is a researched stand-in for a user group, built from interviews or observation across that group. Dana is one office manager's nickname, and the habits are that one person's. No broader research was done, so the card is not a persona and should not settle feature arguments as if it were.

distractorExplanations.b: A real teammate's nickname is not a persona. Using one person's habits as the user group hides the people who were not interviewed or observed.
distractorExplanations.c: A use case needs an actor, a goal, and the path of the interaction. A nickname and a pile of personal habits do not provide that structure.
distractorExplanations.d: A traceability matrix links a requirement to its origin and to a test. A card of one person's habits does not do either.

prompt: A note names a gate agent as the main actor, states a goal of rebooking a missed connection, and writes the main success path plus two alternate paths. A teammate wants to file it as a short user story because a person appears in the first line. Which artifact is the note?

options.text: A user story, because any note that mentions a person and a want is already a story
A persona, because the gate agent is being used as a stand-in for a group of travelers
A use case, because it has a main actor, a goal, and the paths of the interaction
A process model of the whole airline, because two alternate paths were written down

explanation: A use case records a main actor, that actor's goal, the main success path, and the alternate paths. This note does all four for a gate agent rebooking a missed connection. A user story is a short statement of who wants something and why, without those interaction paths. Mentioning a person does not make the note a story.

distractorExplanations.a: A person and a want are not enough to make a user story, and this note is more structured than a story. It already has the main path and two alternates.
distractorExplanations.b: A persona is a researched composite of a user group. The gate agent here is the actor of a specific goal, not a stand-in built from traveler research.
distractorExplanations.d: Two alternate paths do not make a model of the whole airline. The note follows one actor and one goal, which is a use case, not an end-to-end process across roles.

prompt: During Saturday service the analyst drew swimlanes for the host, the server, and the kitchen, with arrows for seating a party, firing the ticket, and running the food. A colleague filed the page as the entity diagram of guests, tables, and dishes. What was actually drawn?

options.text: A data model, because guests, tables, and dishes are what a swimlane diagram is built to show
A process model, because the lanes and arrows show how the work moves between roles
A use case, because the host is an actor and seating a party is that actor's goal
A state diagram of one ticket, because firing and running the food are successive statuses

explanation: A process model shows how work flows, often across roles. These swimlanes and arrows follow seating, firing the ticket, and running the food from host to server to kitchen. An entity diagram would show how guest, table, and dish records relate, which is not what was drawn.

distractorExplanations.a: Guests, tables, and dishes would belong on a data model if the page showed relationships among those records. The page shows handoffs, so filing it as an entity diagram mislabels the flow.
distractorExplanations.c: A use case follows one actor, one goal, and alternate paths. Three roles and the handoffs between them are a process, not a single host goal.
distractorExplanations.d: Firing and running could be statuses of a ticket in a different drawing. Here they are actions moving between swimlanes, which is a flow of work.

prompt: Wholesale clerks need the records to show which customer placed an order, which payment settled that order, and whether one customer can have many orders open at once. They do not need a drawing of who walks a form to the safe. Which model should the analyst draw?

options.text: A process model of clerks walking each paper order from the wholesale counter to the locked safe
A wireframe that sets button colors and label fonts on the wholesale order screen
An affinity diagram of sticky notes from a workshop about what to name the wholesale shop
A data model relating customer, order, and payment, including many open orders per customer

explanation: A data model shows the information the process uses and how those records relate. The clerks need customer, order, and payment, plus whether one customer can hold many open orders. A drawing of someone walking a form to the safe would show flow, which they said they do not need.

distractorExplanations.a: Carrying paper to the safe is a flow of work. The clerks asked how customer, order, and payment records relate, which a process model does not answer.
distractorExplanations.b: Button colors are a screen sketch. They do not show that a payment settles an order or that one customer can have many orders open.
distractorExplanations.c: An affinity diagram groups raw notes. A naming session does not define the relationship among customer, order, and payment.

prompt: The parks department can pay for one small public page and nothing more. The page will not take a fee and will not replace the staff who answer the phone. It counts how many residents attempt to reserve a picnic shelter, so leaders can learn whether a full booking system is worth funding. Which release concept describes this page?

options.text: A minimum viable product, the smallest release that tests whether the value is real
A minimum business increment, the smallest slice that already delivers the business outcome
The finished booking system, because publishing a public page completes the shelter service
A transition requirement, because the page moves reservation work off the phone desk

explanation: A minimum viable product is the smallest release used to test whether the value is real. This page does not take a fee, does not replace the phone staff, and does not complete a reservation. It counts attempts so leaders can learn whether to fund a full booking system. A minimum business increment would be the smallest slice that actually delivers that outcome.

distractorExplanations.b: A minimum business increment delivers a business outcome, such as a completed reservation or fewer calls for the phone staff. This page counts attempts so leaders can decide later, which is a test rather than that outcome.
distractorExplanations.c: A public page that cannot take a fee or replace the phone desk is not the finished booking system. Leaders still have to decide whether to fund the system.
distractorExplanations.d: A transition requirement covers what must be true to leave the old way of working, such as training or a data move. This page leaves the phone desk in place on purpose.

prompt: Last month the clinic turned on a portal meant to reduce missed appointments, posted a launch note, and closed the requirement set. Missed appointments are still as common as they were before the portal existed. The sponsor asks if the effort is finished. How should the analyst answer?

options.text: Treat the launch note as proof the need was met and archive the original case
Start the next clinic feature, because a portal that is already live should not be measured again
Compare missed-appointment results since launch with the need the portal was built to meet
Add the portal's colors to the traceability matrix and mark every linked row as passed

explanation: Shipping is not the end of the analysis. The portal existed to reduce missed appointments, and those appointments are still as common as before. The analyst should evaluate the results against that need. A launch note shows that the portal went live, not that the need was met.

distractorExplanations.a: A launch note records a release. Archiving the case on that basis treats deployment as proof, while the missed-appointment numbers are unchanged.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving to the next feature skips the evaluation. A live portal can still fail the need it was built to meet.
distractorExplanations.d: Colors on a traceability matrix do not measure appointments. Marking rows passed because the site is up confuses a link with an outcome.

prompt: Changing the school lunch menu will be decided by the nutrition director, handled each day by the cashiers in the cafeteria, and felt by students who did not ask for the change. The analyst's list is a single column of names. What should be added to that list before elicitation begins?

options.text: A backlog ranked by which person emailed the nutrition office most recently about the menu
Who decides, who uses the menu change each day, and who is affected without using it
Acceptance criteria for a menu story, even though nobody has written that story yet
A network of cafeteria prep tasks and durations covering the next two lunch-service weeks

explanation: Stakeholder analysis for this work separates who decides, who uses the change, and who is affected. The director decides, cashiers use the new menu each day, and students feel it without having asked. A column of names hides those roles, so elicitation will not know whose decision, whose daily work, and whose impact to seek.

distractorExplanations.a: Email volume is not a role. Ranking names by who wrote recently does not show who decides, who uses the menu, or who is affected.
distractorExplanations.c: Acceptance criteria belong to a story. There is no story yet, and criteria would not classify the director, the cashiers, and the students.
distractorExplanations.d: A task network with durations is a schedule view. It does not say whose agreement, whose daily use, or whose unrequested impact matters.

prompt: Two notes were saved for the returns desk. One says a refund above $200 needs a supervisor's approval before the drawer opens. The other says the cashier prefers a green receipt to a white receipt. Both were labeled business rules. Which note is a business rule?

options.text: The green receipt, because a stated color preference binds how the returns desk must work
Both notes, because each sentence the cashier offered about the drawer or the receipt is a business rule
Neither note, because a constraint on refunds has to be written as a user story first
The refund limit, because it constrains the process no matter which receipt color is preferred

explanation: A business rule constrains the process regardless of personal preference. A refund above $200 cannot open the drawer until a supervisor approves it. That limit binds every cashier. The green receipt is the same cashier's preference, so labeling it a business rule confuses taste with a control.

distractorExplanations.a: A color preference does not constrain the refund. Another cashier can use a white receipt and still run a valid return.
distractorExplanations.b: Not every sentence from the cashier is a rule. The receipt color is a preference, and treating it as a rule would force the desk to follow one person's taste.
distractorExplanations.c: A user story is a need from a user's perspective. The refund limit is already a constraint on the process and does not have to be rewritten as a story to count as a rule.

prompt: Testers walked the enrollment form against the signed specification and every field matched. Employees still cannot do the task that started the effort: choose a health plan that fits a family with two dependents. The analyst has to name the check that has not been done. Which check is missing?

options.text: Validation against the need, because the form matches the spec but the family task still fails
Verification against the spec, because the field-by-field match is the check still open
A MoSCoW downgrade, because a matched spec means the family task was a should-have
A roadmap edit, because the unmet family-plan need belongs in next year's direction rather than in a check

explanation: Verification asks whether the solution was built right against the specification. That check already passed: every field matched. Validation asks whether the right thing was built against the need. Employees still cannot choose a plan for a family with two dependents, so validation is the check that has not been done.

distractorExplanations.b: Verification is the field-by-field comparison with the signed specification, and that comparison already succeeded. Naming it as the open check repeats a finished step.
distractorExplanations.c: MoSCoW classifies priority inside a release. A matched specification does not convert the original family-plan need into a should-have.
distractorExplanations.d: Pushing the need to next year's roadmap avoids the check. The missing step is to judge this form against the need, not to defer the need.

prompt: Nurses reviewed a grayscale intake layout made of boxes and labels, with no save action behind it. The review changed the field order and revealed that an allergy question was missing. A developer plans to release that layout to the ward tonight. What should the analyst call the layout?

options.text: The finished intake product, because nurses already reacted to the field order
A data model, because the boxes and labels are entities and the relationships among them
A wireframe used to elicit requirements, not the finished product the ward should run
A business case, because a grayscale page shows the intake spend is justified

explanation: A wireframe is a model used to elicit, not the finished product. Nurses used the grayscale boxes to change field order and to uncover a missing allergy question, which is the point of showing it. There is no save action behind the layout, so releasing it to the ward tonight would ship a prompt for discussion as if it were the intake product.

distractorExplanations.a: Reaction from nurses is evidence the model worked as an elicitation tool. It does not turn boxes without a save action into the product the ward should run.
distractorExplanations.b: Boxes and labels on a screen sketch are not entities and relationships. A data model would describe the information the intake form stores.
