distractorExplanations.d: A grayscale layout does not compare benefit with cost. Calling it a business case invents a justification the page does not contain.

prompt: Cashiers already have a specified screen that shows an itemized billing statement. Before the desk can open on Monday, those cashiers still need training, and five years of invoices have to be moved out of the old tool. How should the analyst classify the training and the invoice move?

options.text: The same user-facing statement feature, because cutover work is part of that screen
Transition requirements: what must be true to move from the old billing tool to the new one
Nonfunctional requirements, because training and the invoice move describe how fast Monday's desk opens
Acceptance criteria for the statement story, because opening on Monday shows the story is met

explanation: Transition requirements state what must be true to move from the current tool to the new one, such as training and moving existing data. The itemized statement is the user-facing feature and is already specified. Training and the five-year invoice move are not that screen. Without them the desk cannot open on Monday, even if the statement screen is built.

distractorExplanations.a: Cutover work is not the statement feature. Cashiers can have a finished itemized screen and still be unable to open if they are untrained and the old invoices have not moved.
distractorExplanations.c: How fast the desk opens would be a quality target. Training and a data move are conditions of the changeover, not a speed attribute of the statement screen.
distractorExplanations.d: Opening on Monday is a cutover constraint, not the way anyone knows the statement story is met. Acceptance criteria would describe the itemized statement itself.

prompt: Sponsors signed the housing-application requirements in March. In May, caseworkers discovered that an applicant with no fixed address cannot fill a required field, something the earlier conversations did not surface. A teammate argues the March signature bars any further change. What should the analyst do with the May discovery?

options.text: Refuse the discovery, because a signed baseline means later findings cannot change the housing requirements
Edit the March baseline in place and skip the change path, because the address gap is real
Replace the signed baseline with an affinity diagram made from the May caseworker notes
Treat the May finding as open discovery and route the address change through the agreed change path

explanation: Sign-off sets a baseline. It does not freeze later discovery. Caseworkers found in May that an applicant with no fixed address cannot complete a required field, a situation elicitation missed. That finding still has to travel the change path. Silent edits and a hard stop both mishandle a signed baseline.

distractorExplanations.a: A signature establishes the baseline that later changes are judged against. It does not mean a missed situation, such as applicants with no fixed address, is closed to further analysis.
distractorExplanations.b: The address gap is real, and that is why it should be raised. Editing the March baseline in place skips the change path the signature put in force.
distractorExplanations.c: An affinity diagram can group notes. It is not a substitute for the signed baseline, and swapping the baseline for a diagram drops change control.

prompt: A dispatch director asked for a custom map layer after seeing one at a peer agency. The build would cost more than the routing time it would save, and the people on the desk did not request it. The analyst is scoring the request before it enters the backlog. What value should be reported?

options.text: Low, because the benefit does not cover the cost, and a director's wish is not value by itself
High, because a director's request is enough on its own to call the layer valuable
High, because a peer agency already built the same layer and that proves the benefit
Unknowable until the map layer is live, because benefit and cost cannot be compared before the build

explanation: Value is benefit compared with cost. The map layer would cost more than the routing time it saves, and the dispatchers did not ask for it. A director wanting a copy of a peer agency's layer is a wish, not a benefit that covers the spend. The score reported before backlog entry is low value.

distractorExplanations.b: A stakeholder wanting something is not the comparison. Desire without a benefit that covers cost inflates the score.
distractorExplanations.c: Another agency's layer shows that a peer chose to build one. It does not show that this desk's saved routing time covers this build's cost.
distractorExplanations.d: Benefit and cost are already comparable from the estimate in front of the analyst. Waiting until the layer is live skips the score the backlog decision needs.

prompt: An elicitation workshop at the community center produced dozens of loose notes on class times, fees, and childcare. Those notes still need to be grouped by related idea before requirements are written. A planner has begun drawing task boxes, arrows, and durations. Which technique fits that grouping?

options.text: A schedule network, which sequences tasks and durations for the class-planning work
A traceability matrix, which maps each loose note to a test that will cover it
An affinity diagram, which groups the loose notes into related themes
A minimum business increment, which would ship the smallest class that returns value

explanation: An affinity diagram groups many raw notes after an elicitation workshop so related ideas become themes. The community-center notes on class times, fees, and childcare are still loose, and the next step is that grouping, before requirements are written. Task boxes, arrows, and durations are a schedule network, which sequences work rather than clustering notes.

distractorExplanations.a: A schedule network is what the planner started drawing. Sequencing tasks and durations does not group loose notes into themes.
distractorExplanations.b: A traceability matrix links a requirement to its origin and to a test. These notes are not requirements yet, and the step in front of the analyst is grouping, not test coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: A minimum business increment is a small slice that delivers business value. Shipping a class skips the grouping the unsorted notes still need.

prompt: A facilities planner is breaking the clinic renovation into a hierarchy. The parent box is patient rooms. The child boxes are painting, flooring, and lighting, but hallway signage was tucked under that same parent, and the nurse-call wiring that belongs in every room was left out. What must change for this parent box to be valid?

options.text: Remove the hallway signage from this parent and add the nurse-call wiring left out of the rooms.
Keep the hallway signage here and record the nurse-call wiring on a separate side list.
Leave both the signage and the wiring off this parent because painting already stands for the rooms.
Enter the nurse-call wiring under rooms and again under hallways so the same work is listed twice.

explanation: The 100% rule requires the child boxes of a parent to equal that parent: every in-scope piece of the deliverable is present, and nothing outside it is tucked underneath. Hallway signage is not part of patient rooms, so it is extra work on this branch. Nurse-call wiring is room work, so omitting it leaves the parent short. A side list, a single large child, or a double entry does not make the children match the parent.

distractorExplanations.b: A side list leaves the wiring outside the parent, so the children no longer add up to the rooms. Signage that belongs to the hallway is still extra under this box.
distractorExplanations.c: Naming the largest piece does not complete the parent. Painting does not stand in for wiring that is part of the room deliverable, and the signage problem is a separate extra.
distractorExplanations.d: Listing the wiring twice double-counts the same work, so the children are larger than the parent. The 100% rule forbids that overlap as well as gaps.

prompt: On a bridge replacement, the scheduler has a leaf called north abutment concrete and wants to place it on the calendar. A colleague says that leaf is a zero-duration checkpoint, the same kind of marker as the ribbon-cutting. The crew still has to form, pour, and finish that abutment. How should the leaf be treated?

options.text: As a milestone, because a leaf in the hierarchy has no duration of its own.
As the bridge finish itself, because this abutment is the last physical product on the job.
As a summary bar that replaces forming, pouring, and finishing as separately dated tasks.
As a work package that is split into forming, pouring, and finishing activities.

explanation: A work package is the lowest box in the breakdown structure, and it still represents real work. Schedule activities are decomposed from that package so forming, pouring, and finishing can carry dates and durations. A milestone is a zero-duration marker, such as the ribbon-cutting, and it is not a substitute for the abutment package. One package is also not the whole bridge finish, and a summary bar does not erase the activities underneath it.

distractorExplanations.a: Zero duration belongs to a milestone, a point in time. The abutment leaf is a package of work, so treating it as a checkpoint drops the forming, pouring, and finishing.
distractorExplanations.b: One abutment package is a component. Calling it the bridge finish erases the other deliverables that still have to be built and dated.
distractorExplanations.c: A summary bar rolls durations up. It does not replace the activities. Forming, pouring, and finishing still need their own places on the calendar.

prompt: A laboratory crew wants to set the fume hoods while the certifier is still pressure-testing the exhaust ducts. The hoods cannot show a negative reading until that test has fully passed, and starting early would mean pulling the hoods back out. Which dependency should the scheduler keep between the duct test and the hood installation?

options.text: Start-to-start, so the duct test and the hood installation open on the same morning.
Finish-to-start, so hood installation begins after the exhaust test has fully passed.
Finish-to-finish, so the hoods may go in early if both tasks share one end date.
Start-to-finish, so the exhaust test is blocked until the hoods are already set in place.

explanation: Finish-to-start is the usual dependency: the successor does not begin until the predecessor is finished. The hood installation is the successor, and a passed exhaust test is the predecessor. The hoods cannot prove a negative reading while the test is still open, so an overlap would force the crew to pull them back out. The other three links either start the hoods too soon or reverse which task is waiting.

distractorExplanations.a: Start-to-start overlaps the two tasks from the opening morning. That overlap is exactly what the negative-reading constraint will not allow.
distractorExplanations.c: Finish-to-finish ties the end dates and still lets the hoods go in early. Early installation is the rework this room has to avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Start-to-finish reverses the physical constraint. It would hold the duct test until the hoods exist, which is the opposite of the order the certifier requires.

prompt: An exhibit builder compares two chains that both end at the gallery opening. One chain is three fabrication tasks of twelve days each. The other chain is eight labeling tasks of two days each. A coordinator argues that the labeling chain is critical because it contains more tasks. Which chain sets the earliest opening?

options.text: The labeling chain, because eight tasks outnumber three and task count makes a path critical.
Neither chain, because the sponsor picks the opening without using path length at all.
The fabrication chain, since sixteen label days finish before thirty-six build days.
The labeling chain, because many short tasks delay an opening more than a few long ones.

explanation: The critical path is the longest path in time, not the path with the most activities. Three fabrication tasks of twelve days total thirty-six days. Eight labeling tasks of two days total sixteen days. The gallery cannot open before the longer chain finishes, so fabrication sets the earliest opening. A sponsor's preferred date does not replace that length, and crowding a chain with short tasks does not add duration.

distractorExplanations.a: Counting activities confuses the rule. A path with more boxes can still be shorter in calendar time, and the shorter path is not the critical one.
distractorExplanations.b: A sponsor may prefer a date, but the earliest feasible opening is still driven by the longest chain of remaining work. Preference does not erase path length.
distractorExplanations.d: Short tasks do not delay the opening more than long ones just because there are more of them. Sixteen days of labeling finishes well before thirty-six days of fabrication.

prompt: A highway crew can push lane striping four days later and the new lanes still open on the promised Monday. Push that same striping six days later and the Monday opening moves with it. No other task on the opening chain has room to absorb those days. What does the four-day allowance represent?

options.text: How long lane striping can slip before the promised Monday opening has to move.
How long striping can slip before the next crew is delayed, even if Monday still holds.
A required wait that must sit between paving and striping before any paint goes down.
Spare days stored above the baseline for surprises that nobody has identified yet.

explanation: Total float is how long a task can slip before the project finish, or a finish constraint, moves. Four days of striping slip still leave the Monday opening in place, and six days move that opening, so the four days are total float on striping. Nothing in the highway case is a gap before the next crew, a mandatory pause built into the logic, or days held outside the schedule baseline.

distractorExplanations.b: That description is free float, which is judged against the successor rather than against the project finish. This case measures the slip against Monday's opening.
distractorExplanations.c: A required wait inserted on purpose is lag. The four days here are unused room on striping, not a pause the sequence demands between paving and paint.
distractorExplanations.d: Days stored above the baseline for unnamed surprises are management reserve. Total float is schedule room on a task, measured against the finish.

prompt: In a print shop, cover design can shift one day without changing the morning the press is booked to start. Shift cover design by three days and the press start moves, although the ship date still survives because later production steps have room. Which allowance is the one-day figure?

options.text: Total float, because any slip that still protects the ship date is the same allowance.
Lag, a required one-day pause inserted so the press would not start on the design day.
Lead, an overlap that lets the press begin during the final hours of cover design.
Free float: how long design can slip before the press, its successor, has to move.

explanation: Free float is how long a task can slip before it delays the early start of its successor. One day of cover-design slip leaves the press booking intact, so that day is free float. Three days would push the press even though the ship date still holds, which means the room against the project finish is larger than the room against the successor. The one-day figure is the successor limit, not the ship-date limit.

distractorExplanations.a: Total float is judged against the project finish. The ship date surviving a three-day slip shows that total float is larger here. It does not rename the one-day gap before the press.
distractorExplanations.b: Lag is waiting built into the logic on purpose. The one day is unused room the design task may consume, not a mandatory pause the press was required to take.
distractorExplanations.c: Lead pulls a successor earlier so two tasks overlap. Nothing in this case starts the press before cover design finishes.

prompt: After the crew pours an epoxy floor in a commercial kitchen, the manufacturer requires a full day of curing before any cabinet can be set on that surface. The cabinet vendor asks to overlap the cure and start setting boxes on the same afternoon to save a shift. Which schedule element is that mandatory cure day?

options.text: Lead, an overlap that lets the cabinets go in while the epoxy is still curing.
Lag, a required wait inserted after the pour and before any cabinet is set.
Free float on the pour, a day the floor task may skip without pushing the cabinets.
A zero-duration checkpoint named cure complete, with no wait built into the link.

explanation: Lag is waiting time placed between a predecessor and its successor. The epoxy has to cure for a full day before cabinets can be set, and that wait is mandatory even if the pour finishes early. Lead would overlap the tasks, which is the shortcut the vendor asked for and the manufacturer forbids. Unused float can be skipped; this cure day cannot. A milestone can mark the end of the cure, but it does not replace the waiting relationship.

distractorExplanations.a: Lead is overlap, the opposite of a forced wait. Setting cabinets during the cure would violate the manufacturer requirement rather than satisfy it.
distractorExplanations.c: Float is unused room a task may consume. The cure day is required by the product, so it stays on the link even when the pour is early.
distractorExplanations.d: A milestone can mark the moment the cure ends. The day of curing itself is lag on the dependency, not a durationless flag with the wait removed.

prompt: A substation outage plan is drawn two ways for the same breaker swap. One sheet shows horizontal bars across calendar weeks. The other sheet shows boxes linked by arrows and prints no dates on the boxes. The outage lead needs to know what must finish before the breaker swap can begin. Which sheet shows that order?

options.text: The weekly bars, because left-to-right bar order is the dependency logic by itself.
Either sheet, because bar placement and arrow links state the same precedence rule.
The linked boxes, because that drawing shows logical order rather than calendar position.
Neither sheet, because a responsibility matrix is what states which task must finish first.

explanation: A network diagram shows precedence: which task is a predecessor and what must finish before the next task is allowed to start. A bar chart places work on a calendar so the reader can see when activities are scheduled and how long they run. The operator asked what must finish before the breaker swap, which is a logic question, so the linked boxes answer it. Bar position can hint at sequence without stating the predecessor rule.

distractorExplanations.a: A bar chart is a time view. Tasks can be drawn in an order that is not their dependency, and the bars do not by themselves state which task must finish first.
distractorExplanations.b: The two drawings answer different questions. Dates and bar length do not state logic, and arrows without dates do not state the calendar week.
distractorExplanations.d: A responsibility matrix assigns who does the work. It does not show predecessor and successor relationships for the breaker swap.

prompt: A parks department is pricing a new recreation center. Estimators have the final cost of a similar center finished two years ago in a neighboring town, with a comparable pool, gym, and site. They do not yet have quantities for every trade. Which estimating method fits the information they actually hold?

options.text: Analogous estimating, taking the finished neighboring center as the comparison for this build.
Bottom-up estimating, adding a figure for every trade even though the quantities are missing.
Parametric estimating, multiplying a unit rate by quantities the department has not produced.
A three-point estimate, treating that one finished center as the optimistic and pessimistic bounds.

explanation: Analogous estimating uses the actual cost of a prior, similar project when detailed quantities are not available yet. The neighboring recreation center, with a comparable pool, gym, and site, is that comparison. Bottom-up needs the pieces so they can be summed. Parametric needs a rate times a quantity. One historical total is not an optimistic value, a most likely value, and a pessimistic value.

distractorExplanations.b: Bottom-up adds estimates from the pieces of the work. Without quantities for every trade, there is no complete set of pieces to sum, so the data on hand do not support it.
distractorExplanations.c: Parametric estimating needs a statistical rate and a quantity, such as cost per square foot times area. The department has a whole-center comparison, not that pair.
distractorExplanations.d: Three-point estimating needs three judgments: optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic. A single completed center does not supply those three inputs.

prompt: A contractor must price conduit rough-in for a hospital wing. The takeoff shows 4,000 linear feet, and company history says this crew installs 25 feet per labor hour in occupied hospitals. No earlier wing is a close match for the whole job. Which method uses the facts in hand?

options.text: Analogous estimating, treating the crew history as a stand-in for an entire prior wing.
Bottom-up estimating, because a footage takeoff by itself is a sum of every activity cost.
Reserve analysis, reading the feet-per-hour history as a buffer for unknown site conditions.
Parametric estimating, applying the historical install rate to the measured footage.

explanation: Parametric estimating applies a historical rate to a measured quantity. The rate is 25 feet per labor hour and the quantity is 4,000 linear feet, which is enough to price this rough-in without copying an entire past wing. That is different from scaling a similar completed project, from adding independently estimated pieces, and from holding money aside for risk. The feet and the hourly rate are enough to choose the method without first turning them into a total.

distractorExplanations.a: Analogous estimating compares this job with a similar completed project. The prompt states that no earlier wing is a close match, and a productivity rate is not a whole-project analog.
distractorExplanations.b: A takeoff is an input, not the method. Bottom-up would sum separate estimates for each piece of the work rather than multiply one rate by one quantity.
distractorExplanations.c: A productivity rate is an estimating parameter. Contingency and management reserves are allowances for risk, not the feet-per-hour relationship.

prompt: A tunnel team is unsure how long the boring machine will take through mixed ground. The operator can describe a best-case shift, the shift they consider most realistic, and a worst-case shift if they hit the suspected seam. Which inputs does a three-point estimate take from that operator?

options.text: The most realistic shift alone, with the best case and the worst case set aside.
An optimistic duration, a most likely duration, and a pessimistic duration.
The machine budget divided by the crew's planned daily advance through the ground.
One duration copied from the last tunnel that used this same boring machine.

explanation: A three-point estimate is built from three duration or cost judgments: optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic. The operator's best-case shift, realistic shift, and worst-case seam shift are those three inputs. The question stops at the inputs. It does not ask for a triangular average or a weighted PERT result, and a single copied duration or a cost divided by advance would be a different estimating approach.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeping the realistic shift and dropping the extremes leaves a single-point estimate. Three-point work exists to retain the optimistic and pessimistic judgments beside the most likely one.
distractorExplanations.c: Budget divided by a planned advance is a unit-rate calculation. It does not capture the best, realistic, and worst cases the operator can already describe.
distractorExplanations.d: Copying one duration from an earlier tunnel is analogous estimating. It skips the three judgments this crew can make about the mixed ground ahead.

prompt: While planning a port dredging job, the scheduler lists a permit delay that has happened on prior dredges and sets money aside for that delay. A second sum is discussed for problems nobody can name in advance, such as an unlisted wreck under the channel. Which sum is the permit-delay money?

options.text: Management reserve, because a listed schedule threat is funded above the performance baseline.
A change budget that can be opened after the permit delay has already occurred.
Contingency reserve, held for the identified permit delay and kept inside the baseline.
The dredging firm's profit, which has nothing to do with the listed permit threat.

explanation: Contingency reserve covers known risks, the identified items such as a permit delay already seen on prior dredges, and it is included in the baseline. Management reserve is the separate holding for unknown unknowns, such as an unlisted wreck nobody could name while planning, and it sits outside the baseline. The permit-delay money was set aside for a listed threat, so it is contingency, not profit and not a fund that appears for the first time after the delay hits.

distractorExplanations.a: Management reserve is for risks the team could not identify in advance. A permit delay that is already listed is a known risk and does not belong in that holding.
distractorExplanations.b: Contingency is planned into the baseline before the risk occurs. Opening a new budget after the delay hits is a later control step, not the definition of this holding.
distractorExplanations.d: Profit is the seller's commercial margin. It is not the allowance the job holds for a permit delay the scheduler has already written down.

prompt: A finance partner is locking the approved cost baseline for a data hall build. The package already contains the trade estimates plus the allowance for risks the team has logged. The partner also wants to fold in the sponsor buffer for surprises that were never logged. What belongs inside that cost baseline?

options.text: The trade estimates plus the logged-risk allowance, excluding the sponsor surprise buffer.
The trade estimates, leaving both the logged-risk allowance and the surprise buffer outside.
The trade estimates, the logged-risk allowance, and the sponsor surprise buffer, all combined.
The sponsor surprise buffer, with the trade estimates kept in a forecast outside the baseline.

explanation: The cost baseline is the approved budget against which cost performance is measured. It includes the work estimates and the contingency reserve for identified risks. Management reserve, the buffer for unknown unknowns that were never logged, is part of the overall project budget but is excluded from the cost baseline. Folding that buffer into the baseline would hide it inside the measure the team uses for performance.

distractorExplanations.b: Leaving the logged-risk allowance outside drops contingency, which belongs in the baseline. The unknown-unknown buffer is the portion that stays out, not both holdings.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding the sponsor surprise buffer pulls management reserve into the baseline. That reserve is held above the baseline so it is not part of the performance comparison.
distractorExplanations.d: The trade estimates are the core of the baseline. The surprise buffer is the portion that stays outside. It does not replace the estimates.

prompt: At the status meeting for a solar farm build, three figures are on the slide. Figure 1 is the budgeted amount for the tracker rows that should have been finished by today. Figure 2 is the budgeted amount for the tracker rows that are actually finished. Figure 3 is the cash spent so far. Which figure is earned value?

options.text: Figure 1, the budgeted amount for rows the plan said would be finished today.
Figure 3, the cash the solar farm has actually spent up to this status meeting.
Figure 1 minus Figure 3, the gap between planned accomplishment and cash spent.
Figure 2, the budgeted amount for the tracker rows that are actually finished.

explanation: Earned value is the authorized budget for the work that is actually complete. Figure 2 prices the finished tracker rows at their budgeted amount, so it is earned value. Figure 1 prices work that was supposed to be done by the status date, whether or not it is done, which is planned value. Figure 3 is actual cost, the cash spent. Subtracting spend from the planned amount does not produce earned value.

distractorExplanations.a: Figure 1 prices work the schedule said would be finished by today. That is planned value. It does not change when some of those rows are still incomplete.
distractorExplanations.b: Figure 3 is actual cost. Cash spent does not say how much of the budgeted work is complete, so it is not earned value.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracting cash spent from the planned amount mixes two different measures. Earned value is its own figure: the budgeted worth of the rows that are finished.

prompt: On a courthouse renovation, the schedule performance index is 0.86 halfway through the job. The superintendent tells the client that this index is a spending result and asks whether the renovation is under its budget. No spending index is presented. What does 0.86 say about the renovation?

options.text: More of the planned work is finished than the schedule required, so the job is ahead.
Less of the planned work is finished than the schedule required, so the job is behind.
The index is a spending result, and 0.86 means the renovation is under its budget.
The finish should move earlier, because a result under 1 means spare time is available.

explanation: The schedule performance index compares the value of work finished with the value of work planned. A result below 1 means less work has been completed than the schedule called for, so the courthouse renovation is behind. The index does not say whether cash spent was high or low. A result under 1 is a schedule shortfall, not spare time that would justify an earlier finish.

distractorExplanations.a: A result above 1 would mean more work finished than planned. At 0.86 the comparison is below 1, so the renovation is not ahead of the schedule.
distractorExplanations.c: This index is a schedule comparison. Reading 0.86 as an under-budget spending result confuses it with a cost index, which is not the figure in front of the client.
distractorExplanations.d: Being behind does not create an earlier finish. A result under 1 signals that less work is done than planned, not that the date should be pulled in.

prompt: A vaccine clinic rollout shows a cost performance index of 0.91 at the monthly review. The steering group looks at that figure beside the budget for work already completed and asks what it means for those dollars. What does 0.91 say about the completed work?

options.text: Completed work cost less than the budget for that work, so this portion is under budget.
The opening is ahead of its dates, because a figure under 1 means calendar time was saved.
Completed work cost more than the budget for that work, so this portion is over budget.
The figure should be ignored until the rollout ends, because a midcourse ratio has no meaning.

explanation: The cost performance index divides the budgeted value of finished work by what that finished work actually cost. Below 1, the clinic spent more than the budget attached to the work it has completed, which is an overrun on that work. The index does not report whether the opening date moved. It is useful at the monthly review, while there is still time to respond, not only after the rollout ends.

distractorExplanations.a: A result above 1 would mean the finished work cost less than its budgeted value. At 0.91 the rollout is on the overrun side of that line.
distractorExplanations.b: A cost index does not report dates. Treating a value under 1 as saved calendar time confuses this reading with a schedule index, which is a different measure.
distractorExplanations.d: The ratio is meant to show the cost position of work already finished. Waiting until the rollout ends discards the signal while action is still possible.

prompt: A coastal road design runs through a marsh that floods every spring, and the flood would wash out the subgrade. The county still needs the road, but it can shift the alignment onto higher ground a short distance inland. That shift takes the flood off this job entirely. Which threat response is the move to higher ground?

options.text: Avoid, by changing the alignment so the spring flood can no longer hit this road.
Mitigate, by staying in the marsh and adding pumps to cut how often the flood strikes.
Accept, by leaving the alignment in the marsh and recording the flood on the risk list.
Transfer, by insuring the flood while the road stays on the original marsh alignment.

explanation: Avoidance changes the plan so the threat can no longer happen. Moving the alignment onto higher ground means the spring flood cannot wash out this road, while the county still gets a road. The team is not staying in the marsh with a smaller impact, not simply writing the flood down, and not paying a carrier to take the loss. Elimination of the exposure is what makes the shift avoidance.

distractorExplanations.b: Mitigation would keep the marsh route and reduce probability or impact, for example with pumps. The inland shift does not live with a smaller flood. It removes the flood from the work.
distractorExplanations.c: Acceptance leaves the threat in place. Keeping the marsh alignment and recording the flood is the opposite of the shift the county is ready to make.
distractorExplanations.d: Transfer shifts the financial impact to another party while the road would still sit in the flood path. Changing the alignment does not buy that kind of coverage.

prompt: A warehouse owner fears that a fire during construction could destroy inventory stored in the adjacent bay. The builder will not redraw the bay. The owner wants a specialist carrier to take the financial loss if a fire occurs. What is the owner doing with that fire exposure?

options.text: Avoiding it by redrawing the bay so a construction fire can no longer reach the inventory.
Reducing it with another fire watch so both the chance of a fire and the damage fall.
Sending it to the city council as a threat that sits beyond the owner's authority to handle.
Transferring the financial loss to a specialist carrier if a construction fire occurs.

explanation: Transfer moves the impact of a threat to a third party, commonly through insurance or a contract clause. The owner is not changing the bay, cutting the chance of fire, or handing the decision to another authority. The carrier takes the financial loss if a fire occurs. The fire itself can still happen, which is why this is a shift of impact rather than removal of the threat.

distractorExplanations.a: Avoidance would alter the plan so the fire could not affect the inventory. The builder is not redrawing the bay, so the threat remains physically possible.
distractorExplanations.b: Another fire watch would lower probability or impact while the owner still carried the loss. The chosen action is about who pays, not about lowering the chance.
distractorExplanations.c: Escalation fits a threat outside the decision-maker's authority. Buying coverage is within the owner's choice. The city council is not being asked to own this exposure.

prompt: A device maker depends on one overseas chip supplier. A dock strike could stop shipments for several weeks. The team keeps that supplier, qualifies a second factory, and prepays a small buffer of chips. The strike can still happen, yet the line is less exposed. What response did the supply team take?

options.text: Avoidance, because a second factory removes any chance that a dock strike can occur.
Mitigation, cutting the line's exposure while the original supplier stays in place.
Transfer, because the new factory contract moves the strike loss onto that supplier.
Acceptance, because keeping the original supplier means the team took no protective step.

explanation: Mitigation reduces the probability or the impact of a threat that remains in the plan. The dock strike can still occur and the original supplier is still used, but a qualified second factory and a chip buffer make a stoppage less damaging to the line. The team did not eliminate strikes, did not move the loss onto an insurer or a contract counterparty, and did not leave the single-supplier exposure untreated.

distractorExplanations.a: Avoidance would take the threat off the plan. A second source does not stop a dock strike. It reduces how badly a strike hits production.
distractorExplanations.c: Transfer would move the impact to another party through insurance or a contractual shift of loss. Qualifying another factory keeps the response inside the maker's own supply plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Acceptance would leave the single-supplier exposure untreated. Qualifying an alternate and holding chips is an active reduction of impact, not a decision to do nothing.

prompt: A parade organizer lists high wind as a threat but will not change the stand design or buy more anchors. The register sets money aside and states that if wind passes a written speed, crews postpone the parade and use a backup date already held. Which threat response did the organizer record?

options.text: Avoidance, because a backup date changes the plan so high wind can no longer occur.
Mitigation, because a backup date lowers the chance that high wind will arrive that morning.
Acceptance, with funds set aside and a backup date if the wind limit is passed.
Transfer, because the backup date moves the wind impact from the organizer to the venue.

explanation: Acceptance leaves the threat in the plan instead of changing the work to remove or shrink it. Active acceptance pairs that choice with a reserve and a contingent action that runs if the risk occurs. The organizer is not redesigning the stand or adding anchors. The backup date is used if the written wind speed is passed, so the wind is accepted and a triggered action is already named. The wind can still arrive on the original morning.

distractorExplanations.a: The wind can still arrive. A backup date does not change the weather or the stand, so the threat has not been removed from the plan.
distractorExplanations.b: Mitigation would act in advance to reduce probability or impact, such as added anchors. A date used after the limit is passed does not make the wind less likely.
distractorExplanations.d: Nothing in the entry moves the loss to the venue or to an insurer. The organizer still owns the decision to postpone and still uses a date the organizer held.

prompt: During planning for a plant shutdown, the project lead identifies a threat that the national union contract may ban weekend overtime. Settling that contract belongs to the labor-relations director, and the lead has no authority to negotiate it. The shutdown calendar cannot absorb the ban by itself. Which response fits a threat the lead is not allowed to bargain?

options.text: Escalate it to the labor-relations director, who can negotiate what the lead cannot.
Avoid it by rewriting the national contract so weekend overtime is expressly permitted.
Transfer it through a plant rule that forces the union to accept the shutdown calendar.
Mitigate it inside the shutdown crew, treating the contract ban as the lead's own risk to solve.

explanation: Escalation is the response when a threat sits outside the project lead's authority. The national union contract is negotiated by labor relations, not by the shutdown lead, and the shutdown calendar cannot absorb a weekend-overtime ban on its own. The lead should pass the threat to the director who can act on it. Rewriting the contract, inventing a plant rule that binds the union, or treating the ban as an ordinary crew risk all assume authority the lead does not have.

distractorExplanations.b: The lead cannot rewrite a national contract. Avoidance has to be a change the shutdown is actually authorized to make, and this threat is not one of those changes.
distractorExplanations.c: A plant rule cannot compel a union to accept weekend overtime. Transfer uses insurance or a contract clause to shift impact. It does not create bargaining authority.
distractorExplanations.d: Local mitigation assumes the project can reduce the threat. A contract ban enforced above the shutdown is not solved by treating it as the lead's own risk.

prompt: A handheld radio is sold in two models. The basic model has few channels and meets every requirement written for it, with no defects in the latest production lot. The deluxe model adds many channels but misses its specified battery life. A buyer calls the basic model poor quality because it has fewer features. How should the two models be described?

options.text: The basic model is poor quality, because fewer channels mean it missed the written requirements.
Both models share one grade, because quality and grade are two names for the same idea.
The deluxe model is higher quality, because extra channels outweigh the missed battery life.
The basic model is low grade and high quality; deluxe is higher grade but low quality.

explanation: Grade is the feature set assigned to items that serve the same use. More channels make the deluxe radio a higher grade. Quality is conformance to the requirements written for the item being judged. The basic model meets every requirement set for it and has no defects in the latest lot, so it is high quality even with fewer channels. The deluxe model misses battery life, so the added channels do not make it high quality.

distractorExplanations.a: Fewer channels describe a lower grade, not a quality failure. Quality fails when the product misses the requirements written for the model being judged.
distractorExplanations.b: Grade and quality are separate ideas. Feature count can differ while each model is still judged on whether it meets its own written requirements.
distractorExplanations.c: Missing a specified battery life is a conformance failure. Added channels raise the grade. They do not excuse a requirement the deluxe model was supposed to meet.

prompt: A shipyard can spend this month training welders and qualifying the welding procedure before any hull seam is made. It can also wait and x-ray each finished seam to find cracks. The quality lead must fund the step that acts before a defect can exist. Which cost is that step?

options.text: Inspection of finished seams, the step that stops a crack from being created in the first place.
Prevention, the welder training and procedure qualification done before any seam exists.
External failure, treating the training as the cost of cracks found after the ship is delivered.
A warranty payout, using procedure qualification to pay customers for seams that already failed.

explanation: Prevention costs are spent to keep a defect from being created, before the product exists. Training welders and qualifying the procedure happen before any hull seam is made, so that spending is prevention. X-ray of a finished seam finds cracks after the weld exists, which is inspection. External failure and warranty costs come after a defect has reached the customer, which is the opposite timing from the step the quality lead must fund.

distractorExplanations.a: X-ray finds cracks in seams that already exist. That is inspection. It does not stop the crack from being made, and it is not the step that acts before a defect can exist.
distractorExplanations.c: External failure cost is paid when a defect escapes to the customer after delivery. Training before production is the opposite end of that timeline.
distractorExplanations.d: A warranty payout compensates failures that have already reached the customer. Qualifying a procedure is done so those failures are less likely, not as a payment for them.

prompt: The change plan for a stadium project says the project manager may approve extras up to a stated dollar limit. A sponsor now wants a new video board that costs well above that limit and touches the steel. Who reviews this request under the plan the team already approved?

options.text: The project manager alone, because every stadium extra falls inside that personal dollar limit.
The video-board seller, because the firm that suggested the extra is the one that approves it.
The change control board, because this request sits beyond the manager's stated authority.
The site foreman, because the crew hanging the board can approve a steel extra on the spot.

explanation: A change control board reviews changes that the project plan places beyond the project manager's authority. This plan already sets a dollar limit for the manager. The video board is above that limit and it touches the steel, so the request goes to the board. The seller can propose the extra, and the foreman can speak to how it would be built, but neither holds the approval the plan assigned above the manager's limit.

distractorExplanations.a: The plan draws a line at a stated dollar limit. An extra above that line is the kind of change the manager is not authorized to approve alone.
distractorExplanations.b: The seller can propose a change and price it. Approval of a steel extra above the manager's limit belongs to the board named in the plan, not to the firm that would sell the board.
distractorExplanations.d: The crew can advise on how to hang the board. Authority to accept a change of this size is assigned by the change plan, and that plan does not give it to the foreman.

prompt: A library director calls a reading-nook addition small and asks the builder to fold it into the lobby work without touching the opening date or the approved budget. The nook needs new power, another week of finishes, and furniture that was never priced. What must the integrated review examine before anyone says yes?

options.text: Scope, schedule, and cost together, since this add can still move the date and the budget.
Scope wording, because the director already froze the opening date and the approved budget.
Furniture fabric, because the review is limited to finish preferences on an added nook.
The original charter, setting aside the extra finish week and the furniture left unpriced.

explanation: Integrated change control looks at a proposed change across the baselines it will touch, including scope, schedule, and cost. Calling the nook small does not make it neutral. New power, another week of finishes, and unpriced furniture mean the addition can move both the opening date and the budget. A review aimed at wording, fabric, or the original charter would approve scope while ignoring those effects.

distractorExplanations.b: A request to freeze the date does not shrink the review to scope wording. The extra week is evidence that schedule impact has to be examined rather than assumed away.
distractorExplanations.c: Fabric is a finish preference. The integrated review exists to see the combined effect on the work, the calendar, and the money, which this nook has.
distractorExplanations.d: The charter may state the original intent, but the decision in front of the builder is the effect of this addition. Skipping the extra week and the unpriced furniture misses that effect.

prompt: On a museum cafe build, the millwork crew adds heated shelves that no operator requested and that no change request authorized. In the same week the cafe owner emails extra menu boards, and the crew starts building those boards with no decision recorded. What is the heated-shelf addition an example of?

options.text: An approved change, because installing the shelves shows the board already accepted them.
A value-engineering cut that trades planned boards for shelves nobody had specified.
Scope creep, the same pattern as the owner's emailed boards that have no decision logged.
Gold plating, extra features the crew inserted even though nobody asked for them.

explanation: Gold plating is function the team adds even though nobody requested it and no change authorized it. The heated shelves match that pattern. The owner's emailed menu boards are a different problem: unapproved growth pushed from outside the crew, which is scope creep. Installing the shelves does not create an approval that never happened, and adding an unrequested feature is not a controlled cut of planned work.

distractorExplanations.a: No change request authorized the shelves. Doing the work does not create an approval that was never given.
distractorExplanations.b: Value engineering seeks the required function at a lower cost. Adding shelves nobody specified expands the cafe. It does not trade away scope in a controlled way.
distractorExplanations.c: Scope creep is unapproved growth, here the owner's extra boards arriving by email. The shelves were invented by the crew without a request, which is gold plating rather than that outside push.

prompt: A city awards a contract for a fully designed fire station interior. The drawings are complete, and the builder agrees to deliver that interior for one stated price. If lumber prices jump, the builder still owes the city the finished interior at that price. Who carries the cost risk of the lumber jump?

options.text: The city, because a finished design means the buyer repays whatever the lumber actually costs.
The builder, because the stated price leaves any lumber overrun with the selling firm.
Both parties in equal shares, because a stated price splits each overrun down the middle.
The lumber yard, because a fixed price moves material inflation to the firm that sold the wood.

explanation: On a firm fixed-price contract the seller completes a defined scope for a set price and absorbs cost overruns. The interior drawings are complete and the price is stated, so a lumber jump stays with the builder. The city does not reopen the price to repay actual invoices. The contract does not split the overrun in half, and the lumber yard is not the party that promised the city a fixed interior price.

distractorExplanations.a: A finished design supports a fixed price. It does not turn the contract into a repayment of actual lumber invoices. The city pays the stated price.
distractorExplanations.c: A single stated price does not create an equal split. The overrun stays with the party that took the fixed-price obligation, which is the builder.
distractorExplanations.d: The yard may have its own deal with the builder. The city's contract places the interior cost risk on the builder who signed the stated price.

prompt: An archive hires a conservator to stabilize a collection of water-damaged ledgers. Nobody can say how many pages can be saved until the work is under way, so the scope cannot be pinned in a drawing. The archive will pay the hours worked and the materials actually used. Which contract form matches that deal?

options.text: Firm fixed price, with the uncertain page count still delivered for one agreed sum.
Cost plus an award fee, where hours and materials are a bonus paid for finishing early.
Time and materials, paying the actual hours and the materials used on an open scope.
A catalog purchase, treating each damaged ledger as a standard off-the-shelf good.

explanation: Time and materials fits when the buyer cannot define the scope tightly and agrees to pay for the effort and materials actually consumed. The archive does not know how many pages can be saved, so a single fixed sum would force a guess. Paying the conservator's hours and the materials used is that arrangement. An award fee and a catalog purchase describe different commercial deals.

distractorExplanations.a: A firm fixed price needs a scope solid enough for one quoted sum. Page counts that emerge during the work are not that scope, so the fixed-price form does not match the deal.
distractorExplanations.b: An award fee is an incentive judged against performance criteria, not the basic act of paying hours and materials. The archive's deal is payment for effort and materials used.
distractorExplanations.d: A catalog purchase is for a defined standard product. Stabilizing unknown water damage is professional effort with an open quantity, not an off-the-shelf ledger.

prompt: A hotel must open on the posted Friday. The critical interior path is still four days long. The owner authorizes overtime and a second carpentry crew, accepting a higher labor bill so Friday still holds. The phases stay in their original order. Which schedule compression is the owner using?

options.text: Crashing, paying overtime and a second crew to buy the days without reordering the phases.
Fast-tracking, because protecting a posted opening means later phases now run in parallel.
Resource leveling, because a second crew stretches the same hours to avoid an overtime peak.
Lag removal, because the higher labor bill deletes waiting time the original sequence required.

explanation: Crashing shortens the schedule by adding cost on critical-path work, typically through overtime or extra people. The owner is paying a higher labor bill and keeping the original phase order so the Friday opening still holds. Fast-tracking would overlap phases that were sequential and would add coordination risk rather than buy time with money. Leveling usually stretches work to fit a resource limit, and the labor bill is not lag being deleted.

distractorExplanations.b: Fast-tracking runs later work in parallel with earlier work. This case keeps the original order and spends more, so the compression is not an overlap of phases.
distractorExplanations.c: Resource leveling fits the schedule to the resources on hand and often lengthens the path. Adding paid overtime and another crew is a deliberate cost increase to shorten the critical path.
distractorExplanations.d: Lag is waiting inserted between tasks. Nothing here removes a required wait. The four days are bought by paying for more labor on the critical path.

prompt: The approved baseline for a transit shelter says the dry-in date is 12 March. Rain has pushed the realistic dry-in to 19 March. A coordinator edits the baseline file so it now says 19 March, and the variance column returns to zero. How should the dry-in slip be reported?

options.text: Replace the baseline with 19 March so the file matches the forecast and the variance stays at zero.
Delete the dry-in date so no approved day remains for anyone to compare with the rain delay.
Store seven days of lead on the predecessor so the slip is recorded as an overlap, not a late finish.
Keep 12 March as the approved baseline and report the seven-day rain slip as variance.

explanation: Once a baseline is approved, dates are measured against it. The rain moved the realistic dry-in from 12 March to 19 March, and that seven-day difference should stay visible as variance. Rewriting the baseline file so the variance column reads zero hides the slip and bypasses change control. A baseline date changes when a change is approved, not when someone wants the status to look on time. Deleting the date or relabeling the slip as lead also destroys the comparison.

distractorExplanations.a: Matching the file to the forecast hides the delay. A new baseline date needs an approved change. Until then, 12 March remains the measure.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing the dry-in date destroys the comparison instead of reporting it. The commitment should stay visible so the rain impact can be seen.
distractorExplanations.c: Lead is an overlap between tasks, not a place to hide a late finish. Relabeling a seven-day slip as lead misstates both the logic and the variance.

prompt: Three weeks into a clinic-billing release, the sponsor brings a late eligibility rule that would stop real claim denials. The published Gantt shows requirements frozen, and the developers are already mid-sprint on a different goal. What should the team do with the eligibility rule?

options.text: Refuse the rule because the frozen Gantt has already closed scope for this release
Raise the rule for a backlog discussion instead of forcing it into this sprint
Insert the rule into the open sprint tonight so Friday's build contains it
Stop the release and redraw every remaining date before anyone decides on the rule

explanation: The Agile Manifesto ranks responding to change over following a plan, so a late eligibility rule that would prevent real denials is a priority conversation rather than an automatic no to protect a baselined chart. The sprint already has a different goal, so the rule is not dropped into that commitment the same night.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a frozen predictive baseline with a reason to refuse a valuable change. The chart does not outrank a rule that stops claim denials.
distractorExplanations.c: Mixes welcoming a change with silently expanding the sprint. Stuffing the rule into the open sprint rewrites the goal without a product-owner decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats one valuable change as a reason to rebuild the whole release calendar, which is heavier than ordering the rule where it fits.

prompt: A pharmacy director doubts the inventory pilot and will not look at it until the crew delivers a thicker weekly status deck with a screenshot of every screen. A small ordering path already runs against real stock in the test system. What should they put in front of her?

options.text: A longer slide pack that narrates each unfinished module with extra screenshots and commentary
A formal memo that restates the signed scope in contract language before any demo
The ordering path that already runs, using real stock she can try herself
A register of documentation gaps that names an owner and a due date for each missing page

explanation: When a sponsor wants proof, the manifesto places working software above comprehensive documentation. Her doubt is whether the pilot exists as something a pharmacist can use. More slides, a restated scope memo, or a list of missing pages add paper around a path she has not been invited to try.

distractorExplanations.a: Asks for a thicker status deck, which is the documentation the manifesto ranks below a working increment.
distractorExplanations.b: Substitutes a contract-style memo for something she can operate. Restating scope does not show that the pilot runs.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns the request for proof into a paperwork inventory. A gap list describes missing writing, not a usable ordering path.

prompt: The shared tracker has been down since Monday, and a warehouse developer has sat blocked on a label-printer defect with nothing posted for others to see. Teammates keep refreshing the board and will not speak to him until the tool returns. What should a teammate do about the printer defect?

options.text: Talk with the blocked developer about the defect and what is in the way
Wait until the tracker is restored so the impediment can be logged in the official tool first
Require a new ticket template to be filled before anyone is allowed to discuss a blocker
Email the whole department a reminder that every blocker must be typed into the tracker daily

explanation: Individuals and interactions outrank processes and tools. A dead tracker does not replace a conversation with the person stuck on the printer. The board can be updated when it returns; leaving him blocked until then protects the tool and ignores the person.

distractorExplanations.b: Lets a failed tool postpone the conversation. Logging the impediment matters later, and it does not unblock the printer today.
distractorExplanations.c: Puts a process gate in front of talking. A new template is another tool step, not a substitute for asking what is in the way.
distractorExplanations.d: Broadcasts a tool rule to the department instead of speaking with the developer who is actually blocked.

prompt: A city clerk signed a statement of work, then learned the permit form must capture a flood-zone field that residents need at the counter. She is prepared to argue the original contract line by line. The product owner has not yet joined the builders. How should the flood-zone field enter the work?

options.text: Hold the clerk to the signed lines and park the flood-zone field in a formal change order
Let counsel trade redlines for a week before the builders are allowed to hear the field
Add the field quietly and invoice the clerk for stepping outside the signed wording
Have the product owner sit with the clerk and the builders to reshape the need

explanation: Customer collaboration outranks contract negotiation. The flood-zone field is a resident need discovered after signature, so the product owner works it with the clerk and the people who will build it. Holding the old lines, parking the talk with counsel, or hiding the field behind an invoice skips that working session.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the signed statement of work as the last word. A change order may follow, and it is not a substitute for collaborating on the need.
distractorExplanations.b: Hands the shift to contract redlines and keeps the builders out. Negotiation then replaces the collaboration the change needs.
distractorExplanations.c: Hides scope and turns the relationship into a billing dispute. Quietly invoicing the clerk is contract enforcement, not a shared look at the form.

prompt: During refinement of a library catalog, the facilities chief talks over the room and demands that his kiosk story jump ahead of items the product owner already sequenced. The developers start dragging that story toward the top of the list. What should happen to the chief's demand?

options.text: Let the loudest voice win so refinement can end and the developers can start coding
Leave the order with the product owner, who can hear the chief and then decide
Have the developers vote and place the kiosk story wherever the majority of hands land
Ask the scrum master to freeze the sequence so that nobody, chief included, can reorder it

explanation: Ordering the product backlog is the product owner's accountability. A facilities chief may make a case for the kiosk, and volume in the room does not transfer that accountability to the developers, a vote, or the scrum master.

distractorExplanations.a: Hands the sequence to whoever talks over the room. Stakeholder pressure is input, not the ordering decision.
distractorExplanations.c: Moves ordering to a developer vote. The people doing the work select how to build; they do not take the product order away from the product owner.
distractorExplanations.d: Gives the freeze to the scrum master. That role does not own the backlog sequence, and a freeze also blocks the product owner from reordering after hearing the chief.

prompt: On a school-enrollment effort, a director praises the scrum master for being organized and now expects that person to hand each developer a task every morning. The test environment those developers need has been down all day. What should the scrum master spend the morning on?

options.text: Split the morning into named tasks and tell each developer which enrollment story to open
Write the blocked enrollment story personally so the board looks clear before noon
Coach the developers and clear the down environment without handing out their tasks
Collect a personal status from each developer and forward the list to the director before lunch

explanation: The scrum master coaches and clears impediments the team cannot clear. A test environment that has been down all day is that kind of blocker. Choosing tasks each morning belongs to the developers, who manage their own work, and a status packet for the director is not the coaching.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns the scrum master into a task assigner. Developers decide how the enrollment work is picked up; the role does not deal it out each morning.
distractorExplanations.b: Has the scrum master write the story to look helpful. Doing the developers' building removes the impediment from view without coaching them or fixing the environment.
distractorExplanations.d: Converts the role into a status collector for the director. Forwarding a list does not restore the environment or help the developers plan their work.

prompt: A finance manager looks at a loan-calculator story during planning and announces that it is a two-hour task, then tells the developers to record that figure. The people who will build the calculator have not sized the story. Whose figure should be written as the estimate?

options.text: The developers' own size, reached by the people who will build the calculator
The manager's two-hour figure, because a sponsor's number is the one that keeps the plan precise
A blend of the manager's two hours and a quick guess from whoever happens to speak first
A date copied from the release calendar and entered in the plan as though it were the size

explanation: The people who will do the work own both the estimate and the approach. An outside announcement of two hours is not their size, blending it with a first guess still imports that announcement, and a calendar date is a scheduling constraint rather than an estimate of the calculator story.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats a manager's hour figure as the team's estimate. Precision on a slide does not transfer estimating away from the developers who will build the story.
distractorExplanations.c: Launders the manager's number through an average. The first person to speak has not produced the developers' estimate either.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a release date with a size. The calendar can constrain forecasting, and it is not the estimate of this story.

prompt: Monday's session for a restaurant point-of-sale crew is labeled sprint planning, yet the hour goes to collecting what each person finished last week for a steering slide. Nobody states a goal or selects work for the coming two weeks. What should this session produce?

options.text: A status slide the sponsor can read later without attending the register demo
A list of last week's delays with a person's name written beside each late item
Point targets for the next three sprints, printed in large type on the steering slide
A sprint goal and the sprint backlog the developers believe they can finish

explanation: Sprint planning sets why this sprint matters and what the developers will take on, which is a sprint goal plus a sprint backlog. Spending the hour on last week's completions for a steering slide leaves the point-of-sale crew with a status recap and no plan for the timebox.

distractorExplanations.a: Makes the session a status report. A slide the sponsor can read later does not select a goal or the work for these two weeks.
distractorExplanations.b: Turns planning into a blame list of last week's delays. Naming who was late does not create the sprint backlog.
distractorExplanations.c: Asks planning to publish point targets for future sprints. Targets on a slide are not a goal and a backlog for the sprint about to start.

prompt: At 9:15 the airline-gate developers turn one by one toward a visiting project manager and recite the hours they spent. The daily scrum ends before anyone mentions the stuck gate-change story or adjusts the plan for tomorrow. What should these fifteen minutes be used for?

options.text: An hours recital that keeps the visiting project manager's status deck filled in and current
A replan, among the developers, of the next day's work toward the sprint goal
A round of accept-or-reject decisions on stories before anyone is allowed to leave the room
A short process look-back on how yesterday morning felt, packed into the same fifteen minutes

explanation: The daily scrum is the developers' event to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and adapt the plan for the next 24 hours. Reciting hours to a visiting project manager uses up the fifteen minutes and leaves the stuck gate-change story unmentioned, so tomorrow's plan never changes.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns the event into a status report for a project manager. Hours spent are not the replanning the developers came to do.
distractorExplanations.c: Moves product acceptance into the daily scrum. Accepting or rejecting stories is not how the developers replan the next day.
distractorExplanations.d: Folds a retrospective into the morning event. How yesterday felt is a process conversation, not the next-day plan toward the sprint goal.

prompt: Friday on a transit-card effort, the product owner and two riders are in the room. The crew wants both to try the fare slice and to argue about a clumsy stand-up habit, and this hour will not cover both. What belongs in this sprint review?

options.text: A debate on the clumsy stand-up habit and a process experiment the crew will try next sprint
A quiet slide showing of the fare rules, with rider comments postponed to a later written survey
A look at the working fare slice, plus the riders' feedback on what they just tried
A locked commitment for the following sprint, made before anyone has tried the fare slice

explanation: The sprint review shows the increment and invites feedback so the product can be adapted. The riders are in the room to try the fare slice. How the stand-up felt belongs in the retrospective, and locking the next commitment before they try anything skips the inspection.

distractorExplanations.a: Brings retrospective work into the review. A process experiment about stand-up is about how the crew works, not about the fare increment the riders came to see.
distractorExplanations.b: Replaces a working slice and live feedback with a quiet slide showing. Postponing rider comments throws away the inspection this event is for.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the review to commit the next sprint before the increment is tried. The next commitment follows learning, and it is not a substitute for showing the fare slice.

prompt: After a museum-ticketing sprint, the product owner opens the retrospective with a checklist and starts accepting or rejecting each story. The developers came ready to discuss a flaky build server that cost them two days. What should the retrospective examine?

options.text: How the crew works, including the flaky build server that cost two days
Which ticketing stories meet their criteria and can be marked accepted for release
A full reorder of the backlog around a newly requested exhibit-timing feature
Who will own each task in the following sprint before people are allowed to leave

explanation: A retrospective inspects individuals, interactions, process, and tools, then chooses an improvement. The flaky build server is that kind of topic. Accepting stories is a product decision, and it crowds out the two lost days. Backlog order and task assignment are not this meeting.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses the retrospective as an acceptance meeting. Criteria checks belong with the product owner on the items, not in the process improvement event.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the retrospective into backlog ordering. A new exhibit-timing feature is product content, not a look at the build server.
distractorExplanations.d: Makes the meeting a task-assignment session for the next sprint. Naming owners does not improve the way the crew works.

prompt: A new analyst on an insurance-quoting effort keeps placing a multi-month pricing idea onto the sprint backlog because the idea is important, even though the crew already selected a narrow goal for these two weeks. Where should that pricing idea live?

options.text: On this sprint's backlog, because an important pricing idea has to sit inside the current sprint
Inside the sprint goal, stretched until the multi-month pricing idea is fully covered
On a private side list that developers pull from whenever an hour happens to free up
On the product backlog, ordered for a later sprint, outside this two-week plan

explanation: The product backlog is the ordered list of what might be built over the life of the product. The sprint backlog is the goal, the selected items, and the plan for this sprint alone. A multi-month pricing idea can be important and still wait in the longer list until some future sprint selects it.

distractorExplanations.a: Collapses the product backlog into the sprint backlog. Importance does not move multi-month work into a sprint that already has a narrow goal.
distractorExplanations.b: Stretches the sprint goal until the idea fits. The goal is for this sprint, and widening it to a multi-month price change abandons that boundary.
distractorExplanations.c: Creates a shadow queue the developers pull in spare hours. Work then bypasses both the ordered product backlog and the sprint plan.

prompt: The housing-portal sponsor asks what this sprint produced for tenant search. One developer offers a prose slide describing the screens. Another can open a small search that returns real rental units in the test environment. What should the sponsor treat as the increment?

options.text: The prose slide, because it describes every tenant-search screen more completely than a short demo
The small search that returns real rental units and can be tried in the test environment
The falling burndown line, treated as proof of the sprint even while no search path is open
The sprint-goal sentence copied into the release notes and presented as the result itself

explanation: An increment is a usable slice of the product, something a person can operate. The search that returns real units is that slice. A slide, a chart that slopes down, or a goal sentence pasted into notes describes work or intent and is not the result a tenant can use.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a description as the result. A fuller slide still cannot search units, so it is not the increment.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a burndown with the product. A falling line talks about remaining work and does not itself return rental units.
distractorExplanations.d: Promotes the sprint goal sentence into the deliverable. The goal guided the sprint; the notes are not a search a sponsor can try.

prompt: A benefits story meets every acceptance criterion the product owner wrote for that single item. The crew's definition of done still requires each change to be tested and integrated, and this change sits on one laptop, unintegrated. The product owner wants it called done. Which quality bar has the story failed?

options.text: The acceptance criteria, taken as the quality bar that decides whether the increment is finished
The sprint goal, treated as a replacement for both the item criteria and the shared done bar
The definition of done, because the change is not tested and not integrated
The velocity target, treated as a gate that must be hit before any story can be called done

explanation: Acceptance criteria belong to one product backlog item, and this benefits story met them. The definition of done is the shared quality bar for the increment, and here it requires tested and integrated work. A change that still sits on one laptop has missed that shared bar, so it is not part of the increment.

distractorExplanations.a: Collapses every quality bar into the item's acceptance criteria. Those criteria passed; the failure is the shared done bar the laptop change never met.
distractorExplanations.b: Substitutes the sprint goal for both checks. The goal says why the sprint exists and does not replace either the item criteria or the definition of done.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses velocity as a done gate. Throughput from past sprints does not decide whether this change was tested and integrated.

prompt: A Kanban board for a claims desk caps the Building column at three items, and three items already sit there. Five new requests just arrived. A supervisor wants the cap raised so the board looks busy and nothing waits in the ready column. What should the claims desk do with those five requests?

options.text: Finish what is already in Building before pulling any of the five new requests
Raise the Building cap so all five new requests can start and the board looks busy
Start the five new requests now and pause the three items that were nearly finished
Remove the cap entirely so a waiting ready column cannot make the desk look idle

explanation: A work-in-progress limit is how the board pushes finishing. The three items already in Building occupy the cap, so the five requests wait until a slot frees. Raising the cap, starting the five while pausing the three, or deleting the cap adds started work so the desk looks busy and finishes less.

distractorExplanations.b: Raises the limit to look busy. That removes the pressure to finish the three items already in Building.
distractorExplanations.c: Starts more work and stops work that was nearly done. The limit exists so the desk finishes what is in progress before pulling.
distractorExplanations.d: Deletes the limit because a waiting column looks idle. Idle-looking ready work is the point of the cap, not a reason to abandon it.

prompt: A lead on a parking-app crew sees the developers stuck because a vendor certificate is missing, and the lead is the person who can obtain it. The same lead is tempted to rewrite the payment module overnight to demonstrate a preferred coding style. What should the lead do with the missing certificate?

options.text: Rewrite the payment module overnight so the developers can copy the lead's preferred style
Give each developer a different task so the stuck payment module disappears from the board
Leave the missing certificate alone and have the crew estimate a slip around it
Obtain the vendor certificate the crew cannot get, and leave the payment code with them

explanation: Servant leadership removes a blocker the team cannot remove. The certificate is that blocker, and the lead can get it. Rewriting the module overnight takes the coding away to make a point about style, and reassigning or estimating around the certificate leaves the real blocker in place.

distractorExplanations.a: Has the lead rewrite the code to show the preferred style. That displays the lead's skill and pulls the module off the developers.
distractorExplanations.b: Clears the board by handing out different tasks. The certificate is still missing, and task assignment is not the help the crew needs.
distractorExplanations.c: Asks the crew to absorb a slip the lead could remove. Estimating around a blocker the lead can clear is the opposite of taking it off them.

prompt: A backlog item for a campus map says a student can find a building and also save favorites and also message a guide and also export a poster and also book a tour. Estimators cannot settle on a stable size. What should change about this campus-map item before anyone sizes it?

options.text: Keep every behavior in the one item so the student receives all of it in a single release slice
Split it into smaller, separate stories that can be ordered and finished on their own
Convert each of the five clauses into hours by assigning every clause one fixed day of work
Move the entire item into the sprint goal so the crew can display how committed it is
