explanation: A story that chains several behaviors with 'and also' is neither small nor independent, which is why the estimators cannot settle. Splitting gives the product owner pieces that can be ordered, built, and finished separately instead of one unsizable bundle.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps a bundle no one can size, so the student either gets everything at once or the item stays stuck. Independence is what lets the pieces be sequenced.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the clauses into hours. A fixed day per clause does not make the behaviors small or independent, and points or hours still need a story that can be estimated.
distractorExplanations.d: Parks an unsizable bundle inside the sprint goal. Commitment does not fix a story that tries to do five jobs.

prompt: Developers size a payroll story as five points because it feels larger than a two-point story they finished in the previous sprint. A steering member writes that five points means five days and promises that date to the payroll controller. What should that controller be told the five points mean?

options.text: Five person-days of effort, which the payroll controller may treat as a delivery commitment
The fifth working day from today, so the payroll story comes due on that calendar date
A relative size compared with the crew's other stories, not hours and not a date
A headcount of five people who should swarm the payroll story until it is finished

explanation: Story points compare this payroll story with other stories the same crew has sized, here a two-point story from the previous sprint. They are not an hour budget, not a calendar promise, and not a headcount. A date for the controller would need this crew's past throughput, not a translation of five into five days.

distractorExplanations.a: Converts points into person-days and then into a commitment. The five was a comparison with another story, not a promise of five days of effort.
distractorExplanations.b: Reads the point value as a due date on the calendar. Relative size does not say the story falls due on the fifth working day.
distractorExplanations.d: Reads points as people. Five points does not mean five developers should swarm the story.

prompt: A director notes that the grants crew completed 28 points in the latest sprint and the loans crew completed 40, then sets the grants crew a target of 45 so they catch up. The two crews size their own work on different scales. How should the director use the grants result of 28?

options.text: As a forecast aid drawn from what this same crew has finished, not as a score to beat
As a quota the grants crew must raise every sprint until its total matches the loans crew
As evidence that the loans crew is the stronger group and should absorb the grants work
As a promise that 45 points will be finished because the director announced that target

explanation: Velocity is how much this crew finished in past sprints, and it supports a forecast for this crew alone. It is not a target to beat. The loans total of 40 sits on a different point scale, so it cannot show which crew is stronger, and naming 45 does not create 45 points of finished grants work.

distractorExplanations.b: Turns a past result into a quota and a cross-team race. Raising 28 toward 40 or 45 asks the grants crew to beat a number, which is not what velocity is for.
distractorExplanations.c: Compares two crews' point totals. Different scales mean 40 and 28 do not say which group is stronger or who should absorb whose work.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats an announced target as finished work. Velocity records what already happened; it does not make 45 true because a director said it.

prompt: On Wednesday a nurse spots a missing allergy field during a clinic sprint that started Monday with a goal about prescription refills. A developer wants to amend that sprint goal the same afternoon so the field will not be forgotten. Where should the allergy field be recorded?

options.text: Inside Wednesday's rewrite of the sprint goal, so the goal matches the newest clinical discovery
Inside the definition of done, so every remaining refill story quietly grows the allergy field
On the burndown, as extra scope the crew is still expected to absorb before Friday
With the product owner, on the product backlog, kept apart from Monday's refill goal

explanation: Scope discovered mid-sprint that sits outside the sprint goal goes to the product owner for the product backlog. Monday's goal is prescription refills. Amending that goal on Wednesday to absorb an allergy field endangers it. The field is ordered with the rest of the product work rather than hidden in the done bar or piled onto the burndown.

distractorExplanations.a: Rewrites the sprint goal the afternoon the field appears. New scope is not added to the goal the crew already selected.
distractorExplanations.b: Hides the field inside the definition of done. That bar is a shared quality check, not a pocket for a newly found data element.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops the field onto the burndown as scope to absorb by Friday. The chart shows remaining work; it is not a side door into the sprint.

prompt: Nobody on the tax crew knows whether a legacy API can return amended returns. They propose a three-day spike. A stakeholder asks them to tuck a small filing feature into those three days so the time produces more than research. What should that spike produce?

options.text: The filing feature, shipped under a research label so the three days still count as delivery
A timeboxed answer about whether the API can return amended returns, and no hidden feature
A design of the entire tax module that continues past the third day if the questions remain open
Velocity credit, recorded by treating the research time as finished product scope on the board

explanation: A spike is a timeboxed investigation bought to answer a question, here whether the legacy API can return amended returns. When the three days end, the crew should know that answer. It is not a disguise for a filing feature, an open-ended design of the whole module, or a way to mint velocity from research.

distractorExplanations.a: Hides a feature inside the spike. The stakeholder's filing request is product scope and does not belong under a research label.
distractorExplanations.c: Removes the timebox. A design that runs past the third day until the whole tax module is sketched is no longer a spike.
distractorExplanations.d: Counts research as finished product so velocity rises. A spike produces information, not a slice of the product to score.

prompt: The support-portal burndown looks jagged because the crew split a story after learning something new. A manager wants tasks reshuffled until the line looks smooth in the steering pack, although real work remains on the board. What should the crew do with the jagged line?

options.text: Reshuffle tasks until the line slopes evenly, so the steering pack looks under control
Hold the sprint open until the line can touch zero along a neat diagonal for that pack
Use the chart to talk about work still left, and leave the jagged line as it is
Send the smoothed chart to the manager instead of discussing the stories still on the board

explanation: A burndown is a conversation about remaining work. Splitting a story after new information should move the line, including making it jagged. Smoothing it for a steering pack, holding the sprint open for a neat diagonal, or mailing the picture in place of the conversation hides the work the chart is there to show.

distractorExplanations.a: Makes a pretty line the goal. Reshuffling tasks so the pack looks calm conceals the remaining support-portal work.
distractorExplanations.b: Extends the sprint to suit the graphic. The chart does not decide the timebox, and a neat zero is not the purpose.
distractorExplanations.d: Replaces the conversation with a mailed picture. The manager then sees a curve and never hears which stories are still open.

prompt: A two-week iteration on a court-docket tool is scheduled to close on Friday. Several stories are still open, and a developer wants that same iteration held open until the following Monday so the product slice can be finished first. Which of these ends on Friday anyway?

options.text: The iteration, which still closes on Friday with docket stories open
The product slice, which ends on Friday once every planned docket story is already usable
No scheduled boundary, until the product owner declares the open docket stories complete
The product backlog, which is cleared and retired when Friday's timebox is reached

explanation: An iteration is the timebox, and it ends when the time ends. Friday still closes this two-week iteration whether or not the docket stories are finished. The increment is the usable product slice, a different thing from the container of time, and unfinished work does not keep the container open through Monday.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the increment with the iteration. The product slice is what got built; it does not define when the timebox ends, and it does not wait on every planned story before Friday can arrive.
distractorExplanations.c: Says nothing ends until the product owner calls the stories complete. The timebox is not held open by unfinished work.
distractorExplanations.d: Retires the product backlog at the timebox. That ordered list lives on past Friday; the iteration is what ends.

prompt: Friday arrives for a utility-outage sprint and two stories are still open. A developer suggests sliding the end to Tuesday without an announcement, so those stories stay on the sprint backlog and the shortfall goes unmentioned. What should happen to those two stories?

options.text: They remain inside a sprint whose end slides from Friday to Tuesday until both are finished
They are marked done, because the timebox expired and the crew already spent effort on them
They become the definition of done that the following sprint is required to satisfy
They return to the product backlog so the product owner can order them again

explanation: When the timebox ends, unfinished work is not done. It returns to the product backlog, where the product owner orders it against everything else. Quietly moving Friday to Tuesday drops the fixed length of the sprint and hides those two outage stories from that ordering.

distractorExplanations.a: Extends the sprint in silence. The end does not slide to Tuesday so open stories can remain on the sprint backlog.
distractorExplanations.b: Marks effort as done because the clock ran out. Spent time without a finished story does not meet the bar, so the stories are not done.
distractorExplanations.c: Promotes unfinished stories into the definition of done. That bar is a quality agreement, not a parking place for the two open items.

prompt: A story on the lab-results crew meets the acceptance criteria walked through in the review. A department head asks the scrum master to sign that story the way a manager signs a deliverable. The product owner is present and has not spoken. Who should accept the item?

options.text: The scrum master, signing the story for management the way a deliverable gets signed
The product owner, judging the item against its acceptance criteria
The developers on their own, with no product-owner look at those acceptance criteria
The department head, because acceptance has to travel the organizational approval chain

explanation: The product owner accepts a product backlog item by judging it against its acceptance criteria. A scrum master who signs like a manager is playing an approval role the framework does not give that person, and a department head's chain does not replace the product owner who is already in the room.

distractorExplanations.a: Makes the scrum master a signing manager. That role coaches and clears impediments; it does not accept the lab-results story.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaves acceptance with the developers alone. They build the item, and the product-owner judgment against the criteria is still required.
distractorExplanations.d: Routes acceptance through a department hierarchy. Organizational sign-off does not replace the product owner on the item's criteria.

prompt: Each Monday a coordinator on a fleet-maintenance effort hands every developer a personal assignment list and then checks those lists inside the daily scrum. The calendar invite calls this coordinator the scrum master. What is that Monday assignment list an example of?

options.text: Scrum master, because the person who runs the morning meeting holds that role by default
Product owner, because dealing out Monday assignments is how the backlog receives its order
A coordinator assigning daily tasks, which is not the scrum master role
Servant-leader, because checking each personal list is how impediments get removed

explanation: Scrum has no project manager who hands out the day's tasks, and the scrum master does not take that job either. Developers manage their own work. A calendar label does not turn Monday assignment lists into the scrum master role, which is coaching and impediment removal.

distractorExplanations.a: Equates the role with whoever is named on the invite and stands in the morning meeting. The behavior is task assignment, not the scrum master role.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses handing out tasks with ordering the backlog. The product owner orders product work; a personal Monday list is neither that order nor that role.
distractorExplanations.d: Calls list-checking servant leadership. Looking over assignments is supervision, not removing a blocker the crew cannot remove.

prompt: In planning poker for a bridge-inspection story, the cards show 2, 3, 8, and 13. The facilitator averages those cards to 6.5 and moves to the next story before the person who showed 13 can mention a permit risk the others did not know about. What should happen before this story receives a size?

options.text: The crew discusses why the cards differ, hears the permit risk, and votes again
The first silent cards are averaged to 6.5 so the planning clock can keep moving
The lowest card is kept so the inspection story looks small enough to enter the sprint
The highest card is converted into hours and sent to the sponsor for approval

explanation: Planning poker is there to expose disagreement. A spread from 2 to 13 means the estimators do not share one picture, and the 13 is a reason to talk, especially about a permit risk the others missed. Averaging the first silent round records a size nobody argued for and buries that risk.

distractorExplanations.b: Averages the opening cards and moves on. The 6.5 hides the spread and skips the permit risk that the high card was signaling.
distractorExplanations.c: Lowballs the story to make it fit. The smallest card is not the size, and it also skips the conversation about why someone said 13.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns the high card into hours for a sponsor approval. Points from one round are not an hour request, and the spread still needs a discussion before any size is kept.

prompt: Thursday afternoon a voter-roll crew spends time refining three upcoming stories, splitting one of them, and clarifying acceptance criteria. They choose no sprint goal. A manager says the next sprint is now committed because the stories look ready. What did Thursday's session settle?

options.text: A commitment to the next sprint, on the view that ready stories already form a sprint backlog
A cancellation of Monday planning, because refinement stood in for that event
Acceptance of the three stories, as if clearer criteria were the same thing as a signature
Preparation of upcoming items, with no sprint goal chosen and no sprint committed

explanation: Backlog refinement is ongoing preparation: splitting, clarifying, and sizing items the crew might choose later. It is not sprint planning. Looking ready helps a future planning session and does not create a sprint goal or a commitment, so Monday's planning is still the event that selects the sprint.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats refined stories as a committed sprint backlog. Ready is not the same as selected for a sprint that has no goal yet.
distractorExplanations.b: Cancels sprint planning because refinement happened. Refinement prepares items; it does not replace the event that commits the sprint.
distractorExplanations.c: Reads clearer acceptance criteria as acceptance. Clarifying what a voter-roll story means does not mean the product owner has accepted it.

prompt: A program office asks the scholarship crew to add a weekly status meeting so leaders can learn which stories are blocked. A board on the team-room wall already shows the goal, the items in progress, and the blockers to anyone who walks past. How can those leaders see the blockers without adding a meeting?

options.text: Add a second weekly meeting in which each person reads that same wall board out loud
Have the leaders read the wall board, which already shows the blockers in the open
Take the wall board down and email a slide that is reserved for the program office
Turn the daily scrum into a leadership briefing and retire the wall board afterward

explanation: An information radiator is a visible display of the work's state, meant to be read without calling a status meeting. The scholarship board already shows blockers to anyone walking past. Reading it aloud in another meeting, hiding it in email, or converting the daily scrum into a briefing gives up the reason the board is on the wall.

distractorExplanations.a: Schedules a meeting to narrate a board people can already read. That recreates the status meeting the wall was supposed to make unnecessary.
distractorExplanations.c: Hides the state in a private slide. A radiator works because anyone can see it, not because one office receives a copy.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns the developers' daily scrum into a briefing for leaders and then removes the board. The morning event is not a status meeting, and retiring the board removes the radiator.

prompt: A medical-device effort must clear a fixed regulatory gate on a date the agency set, using evidence the agency named beforehand. Inside that gate the crew builds the device software in short iterations and shows a working slice every cycle. Which portion of the effort is being run in an agile way?

options.text: The entire effort, so the agency date should move whenever one of the working slices runs late
The regulatory gate itself, because a fixed agency date is simply another kind of sprint goal
The software build inside the gate, where each cycle shows a working slice
No portion at all, because a hybrid effort drops both the fixed date and the short cycles

explanation: A hybrid effort can keep a predictive gate where the constraint is real: the agency date and the named evidence stay fixed. The agile portion is the build inside that gate, done in short cycles that show a working slice. Iterating does not erase the gate, and the gate does not become a sprint goal merely by sitting on a date.

distractorExplanations.a: Collapses the hybrid into agile everywhere, then flexes the agency date. The regulatory gate stays predictive even while slices are shown inside it.
distractorExplanations.b: Calls the fixed gate a sprint goal. A date and an evidence list set by the agency are the predictive part, not the iterative build.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops both the plan and the iterations. Hybrid work keeps the gate and keeps the cycles; it does not abandon either one.
